investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: On a non-contrast CT head, is acute blood hyperdense or hypodense, and how does its appearance change over time?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: Acute haemorrhage is HYPERDENSE (bright/white). It becomes isodense (~1 week) then HYPODENSE (dark) when chronic. So a dark extra-axial collection is an old/chronic bleed.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: How do you distinguish an extradural from a subdural haematoma on CT by shape?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Extradural = biconvex/lentiform, does NOT cross suture lines (arterial, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval).
  • Subdural = crescent-shaped, DOES cross sutures (bridging veins; elderly, alcohol, anticoagulants).

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: What is the first-line role of a non-contrast CT head in suspected acute ischaemic stroke?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: To exclude intracranial HAEMORRHAGE before giving thrombolysis. Early ischaemia is often invisible, so a normal CT does not exclude stroke.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: List the early (subtle) CT signs of acute ischaemic stroke.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Loss of grey-white differentiation
  • sulcal effacement
  • insular ribbon sign
  • and the hyperdense MCA sign (visible thrombus).
Established infarct = wedge-shaped hypodensity in a vascular territory.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: A patient with thunderclap headache has a normal CT head. Does this exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: No. A normal CT does not exclude SAH. If clinical suspicion persists, perform a lumbar puncture at ≥12 hours from onset looking for xanthochromia.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Why does a lesion "enhance" on contrast-enhanced CT head?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: IV iodinated contrast normally stays intravascular behind an intact blood-brain barrier. A lesion enhances when it disrupts the BBB (tumour, abscess, subacute infarct, active demyelination) or is intrinsically vascular / lacks a BBB (meningioma, AVM). Enhancement therefore marks BBB breakdown or high vascularity.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Give the mnemonic for ring-enhancing brain lesions and the top three to distinguish.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
MAGIC DR:
  • Metastasis
  • Abscess
  • Glioblastoma
  • Infarct (subacute)
  • Contusion
  • Demyelination
  • Radiation necrosis / Resolving haematoma.
The top three to distinguish at finals are cerebral abscess, glioblastoma and metastases.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: How do you distinguish cerebral abscess from glioblastoma on imaging?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Abscess: thin, smooth, regular enhancing ring with central restricted diffusion on MRI DWI, plus systemic sepsis.
  • GBM: thick, irregular, nodular ring with central necrosis that crosses the midline via the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma).

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: What safety checks are needed before giving IV iodinated contrast for a CT head?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Check renal function (eGFR/U&E) for contrast-induced nephropathy risk and ensure hydration
  • ask about previous contrast reaction/allergy and asthma/atopy (anaphylactoid risk)
  • consider metformin (withhold around contrast if renal impairment).
Also consider whether MRI with gadolinium would be more appropriate.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: How does a meningioma typically appear on contrast CT, and why?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: An extra-axial, dural-based mass showing homogeneous (avid, uniform) enhancement, often with a dural tail. It enhances strongly because it is highly vascular and lacks a blood-brain barrier, not because of BBB breakdown.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: What is the primary purpose of the first-line non-contrast CT (NCCT) in the acute stroke protocol?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: To exclude intracranial haemorrhage, because management of ischaemic vs haemorrhagic stroke diverges completely (thrombolysis is contraindicated if there is blood). It also shows early ischaemic signs.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: List four early ischaemic signs on non-contrast CT.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Loss of grey-white differentiation
  • loss of the insular ribbon (insular ribbon sign)
  • sulcal effacement
  • and the hyperdense MCA/vessel sign (visible thrombus).
ASPECTS quantifies MCA-territory change.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: What does CT angiogram (CTA) add, and which patients does it identify?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: CTA maps the vessels to detect a large vessel occlusion (LVO) — proximal MCA, ICA or basilar — identifying patients suitable for mechanical thrombectomy.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: On CT perfusion, what is the difference between core and penumbra, and why does the mismatch matter?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Core = irreversibly infarcted tissue
  • penumbra = salvageable at-risk tissue.
A large mismatch (small core, big penumbra) selects patients for reperfusion in the extended window (thrombectomy up to ~24h).

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Give the time windows for thrombolysis and thrombectomy in ischaemic stroke.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Thrombolysis (IV alteplase/tenecteplase): generally within 4.5h of onset.
  • Thrombectomy for LVO: up to ~6h, extended to ~24h if perfusion imaging shows favourable core/penumbra mismatch.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: What are the two most important clinical uses of a CT angiogram of the Circle of Willis at finals level?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• (1) Localising a ruptured aneurysm as the cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage (to plan coiling/clipping)
  • and (2) identifying a large-vessel occlusion in acute ischaemic stroke (to plan thrombectomy).

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: List the three commonest sites of berry (saccular) aneurysms, in order of frequency.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: Anterior communicating artery (ACom, commonest) > posterior communicating artery (PCom) > middle cerebral artery (MCA) bifurcation.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Outline the imaging pathway for a suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Non-contrast CT head first (blood in basal cisterns).
  • If negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture at ≥12 hours for xanthochromia.
  • If SAH is confirmed, CTA (or DSA) to find the aneurysm.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Which aneurysm classically causes a painful third nerve palsy with a fixed dilated pupil, and why?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: A posterior communicating artery (PCom) aneurysm — it lies next to CN III and compresses the superficial parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres, giving a 'surgical' third nerve palsy with a fixed dilated pupil.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Name three major complications of aneurysmal SAH and the drug used to reduce one of them.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Re-bleeding (secure the aneurysm early)
  • vasospasm/delayed cerebral ischaemia
  • and hydrocephalus.
Nimodipine is given to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: What is the main indication for a CT venogram (CTV) of the head?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: Suspected cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) — CTV times contrast to opacify the dural venous sinuses and cerebral veins to look for a filling defect.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: What is the 'empty delta sign' and where is it seen?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: On contrast CTV, contrast enhancement surrounds a central non-enhancing clot in the superior sagittal sinus, giving a triangular 'empty' centre — a classic sign of CVST.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: On a non-contrast CT, what two signs suggest cerebral venous sinus thrombosis?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• A hyperdense (dense) sinus from acute clot
  • and the cord sign (a hyperdense thrombosed cortical vein).

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: List the key prothrombotic risk factors for CVST.
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Pregnancy/puerperium
  • combined oral contraceptive pill
  • thrombophilia
  • dehydration
  • malignancy
  • and local sepsis (mastoiditis/sinusitis → cavernous/transverse sinus)
  • also head injury.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: How is CVST managed if there is an associated haemorrhagic venous infarct?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: Still anticoagulate — LMWH then oral anticoagulation, even with venous haemorrhage — plus treat seizures and raised ICP and address the underlying cause.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: On CT perfusion, which parameters define the infarct CORE?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: Markedly reduced CBF together with reduced CBV — a MATCHED defect. Volume has collapsed because autoregulation is exhausted, so the tissue is irreversibly infarcted.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: On CT perfusion, which parameters define the salvageable PENUMBRA?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: Prolonged MTT/Tmax with relatively PRESERVED CBV (autoregulation still maintaining blood volume). This perfusion-core mismatch marks tissue at risk but still viable.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Which two mismatch criteria extend thrombectomy into the late window, and to what time?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back:
• Clinical-core mismatch (up to ~24h)
  • and perfusion mismatch (6–16h).
Both select patients with a small core and a large salvageable penumbra, extending mechanical thrombectomy to about 24 hours from onset.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Where does CT perfusion sit in the acute stroke imaging protocol?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: NCCT (exclude haemorrhage) → CTA (locate the occlusion) → CTP (quantify core vs penumbra). CTP complements but does not replace the plain scan and angiogram, and must not delay treatment of early-window candidates.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.front: Why does a large established core argue against reperfusion?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.back: Little tissue is salvageable, so benefit is low, while the risk of haemorrhagic transformation of the already-infarcted core is high. A favourable outcome requires a small core with a large mismatch.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What is the standard technique and imaging plane for a routine CT of the paranasal sinuses, and why?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Non-contrast, thin-slice CT reformatted in the coronal plane. The coronal plane best demonstrates the ostiomeatal complex (OMC), the key drainage pathway assessed before FESS.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: On CT sinuses, how do you distinguish acute from chronic sinus disease?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• An air-fluid level within a sinus indicates acute infection.
  • Bony sclerosis and thickening of the sinus walls indicate long-standing chronic rhinosinusitis.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Name four anatomical variants on pre-FESS CT sinuses that increase surgical risk, and what each endangers.
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Dehiscent lamina papyracea (orbital breach)
  • Onodi cell (posterior ethmoid cell abutting the optic nerve)
  • Haller/infraorbital ethmoid cell (narrows OMC)
  • and an asymmetric/low ethmoid roof or cribriform plate (CSF leak / intracranial injury).

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: A CT shows unilateral sinus opacification with bony destruction. What must be excluded?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Sinonasal malignancy and invasive fungal sinusitis. In a diabetic or immunocompromised patient this is mucormycosis until proven otherwise; add contrast CT/MRI to assess soft tissue and orbital/intracranial spread.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Which complication of ethmoid sinusitis threatens vision, and what CT-detectable signs suggest it?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
Orbital cellulitis / subperiosteal abscess (spread through the thin lamina papyracea). Signs:
  • proptosis
  • restricted/painful eye movements
  • reduced acuity
  • and a subperiosteal collection displacing the medial rectus.
It is an emergency requiring urgent contrast imaging, IV antibiotics and ENT/ophthalmology referral.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: How do you clinically distinguish preseptal from orbital (post-septal) cellulitis?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Preseptal: eyelid swelling only, NO proptosis, painless full eye movements, normal acuity/colour vision (oral antibiotics).
  • Orbital/post-septal: proptosis, PAINFUL/restricted eye movements, reduced acuity and colour vision, chemosis — a sight- and life-threatening emergency (IV antibiotics, CT, urgent ophthalmology).

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What is the 'teardrop sign' on CT orbits and which muscle can be entrapped in a blowout fracture?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: The teardrop sign is herniated orbital fat and/or inferior rectus prolapsing through an orbital floor fracture into the roof of the maxillary sinus. Inferior rectus entrapment causes restricted upgaze and vertical diplopia; also test infraorbital nerve sensation (cheek numbness).

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Why must you avoid MRI if an intra-orbital foreign body may be present, and what imaging is preferred?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: A ferromagnetic (metallic) foreign body can be moved by the magnetic field, damaging the globe/optic nerve and causing blindness. Use CT (excellent for radio-opaque metal and glass); exclude a metallic FB with CT or plain films before any MRI.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What CT feature of the extraocular muscles suggests thyroid eye disease, and which muscles are typically affected?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Enlarged muscle BELLIES with SPARING of the tendon insertions (unlike orbital myositis). Order of involvement 'IM SLow': Inferior > Medial > Superior > Lateral rectus. Apical crowding can compress the optic nerve.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What is a paediatric 'white-eyed' trapdoor blowout fracture and why is it an emergency?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: A greenstick orbital floor fracture in a child with minimal bruising/swelling ('white eye') that traps the inferior rectus. It can trigger the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea/vomiting) and cause muscle ischaemia — needs urgent surgical release.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What is the key CT feature distinguishing cholesteatoma from a simple middle ear effusion?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Cholesteatoma is a NON-dependent soft-tissue mass (typically in the attic/Prussak's space) that causes BONY EROSION — classically blunting of the scutum and erosion of the ossicles. An effusion is dependent and does not erode bone.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What CT sign defines coalescent mastoiditis (as opposed to simple mastoid opacification)?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Loss of the fine bony septa between the mastoid air cells (coalescence), often with a subperiosteal abscess. Opacification of the air cells alone is not enough to diagnose surgical mastoiditis.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Contrast longitudinal and transverse temporal bone fractures.
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Longitudinal (commoner): runs along the long axis of the petrous bone; causes ossicular disruption → conductive hearing loss and CSF otorrhoea.
  • Transverse: runs across the axis (through the otic capsule); causes sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo and a higher risk of facial nerve injury.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: List the danger complications of cholesteatoma/mastoiditis to actively look for on temporal bone CT.
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Facial nerve palsy (erosion of the facial canal)
  • labyrinthine fistula (usually eroding the lateral semicircular canal → vertigo)
  • tegmen erosion
  • and intracranial spread — meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and cerebral/extradural abscess.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What anatomical structures does HRCT of the petrous temporal bone assess, and its main clinical indications?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Structures: external/middle/inner ear, ossicles, mastoid air cells, facial nerve canal and otic capsule.
  • Indications: cholesteatoma, complicated/chronic otitis media and mastoiditis, conductive hearing loss, temporal bone trauma, pre-cochlear-implant assessment and CSF leak.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What is the imaging investigation of choice for maxillofacial trauma, and why?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Thin-slice CT of the facial bones with multiplanar reformats (and often 3D reconstruction). It maps the fracture pattern in 3D to plan surgical fixation and detects associated orbital, skull-base and C-spine injuries missed on plain films.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What anatomical structure is crossed by ALL Le Fort fractures?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
The pterygoid plates.
  • Le Fort I = horizontal ("floating palate")
  • Le Fort II = pyramidal through the nasofrontal region and infraorbital rims ("floating maxilla")
  • Le Fort III = craniofacial disjunction ("floating face").

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Which sutures/bones are fractured in a ZMC ("tripod") fracture, and what are the typical clinical signs?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Zygomaticofrontal suture
  • zygomatic arch
  • and infraorbital rim/anterior maxillary wall.
Signs:
  • cheek (malar) flattening
  • infraorbital nerve numbness of the cheek and upper lip
  • and trismus.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Why should you always look for a second fracture on a mandible CT?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: The mandible is a ring ("ring bone"), so it commonly fractures in two places. If one fracture is seen, actively search for a second body/angle fracture or a condylar fracture.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Name three airway/vision red flags in facial trauma requiring urgent action.
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• 1) Airway obstruction from bleeding, displaced midface fractures, or a bilateral parasymphyseal 'flail' mandible causing tongue fall-back (manage ABC/C-spine first).
  • 2) CSF rhinorrhoea indicating base-of-skull injury.
  • 3) Retrobulbar haemorrhage or muscle entrapment threatening vision (sight-saving emergency).

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: On contrast-enhanced CT neck, what appearance distinguishes a drainable abscess from cellulitis/phlegmon?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• An abscess is a rim-enhancing collection with central low density (fluid/pus) and surrounding fat stranding
  • cellulitis/phlegmon is ill-defined enhancement with no drainable cavity.
Gas locules suggest necrotising infection.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Why is a retropharyngeal abscess particularly dangerous, and what CT finding must you actively look for?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: It lies in the "danger space" and can track inferiorly to the mediastinum, causing mediastinitis. Always follow the collection caudally on sagittal/coronal images to check for mediastinal extension.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What are the CT features of a malignant lymph node in head & neck cancer staging?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Enlarged, rounded (loss of normal oval shape)
  • central necrosis (low-density centre)
  • loss of the fatty hilum
  • and extranodal/extracapsular spread with irregular margins.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What is Ludwig's angina and why is it a CT/airway emergency?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Bilateral submandibular and sublingual space cellulitis, usually odontogenic. It elevates and displaces the tongue causing rapid airway compromise — secure the airway (senior anaesthetics/ENT) plus IV antibiotics and drainage.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: A CT neck for tonsillitis shows an internal jugular vein filling defect. What syndrome, organism, and management?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Lemierre's syndrome — septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically Fusobacterium necrophorum. Needs prolonged IV antibiotics, with anticoagulation considered; watch for septic pulmonary emboli.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: After a TIA or non-disabling ischaemic stroke in the anterior circulation, what carotid imaging pathway is used?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Image the carotids urgently: Doppler ultrasound first-line, with CTA or MRA to confirm and quantify stenosis. Symptomatic significant stenosis on the appropriate side is referred for carotid endarterectomy.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What degree of symptomatic carotid stenosis warrants endarterectomy, and within what timeframe?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: Symptomatic stenosis of ~50–99% (NASCET, per NICE) on the side appropriate to symptoms → carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of symptom onset, plus best medical therapy. A 100% occluded carotid is not revascularised.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What is 'best medical therapy' for carotid stenosis / secondary stroke prevention?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
• Antiplatelet therapy
  • a high-intensity statin
  • blood pressure control
  • and smoking cessation (plus diabetes and lifestyle optimisation).

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: What CTA findings and clinical triad suggest carotid dissection?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back:
CTA:
  • tapered 'flame'/string sign of luminal narrowing
  • an intimal flap
  • or a false lumen from intramural haematoma.
Triad: neck/head pain + partial (painful) Horner's syndrome (ptosis + miosis) + cerebral/retinal ischaemia. A cause of stroke in the young; treat with antiplatelet or anticoagulation.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.front: Why does carotid dissection cause a partial Horner's syndrome rather than a full one?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.back: The expanding vessel wall disrupts the sympathetic fibres running along the internal carotid, causing ptosis and miosis (painful). Sudomotor fibres to the face travel mainly along the external carotid, so facial anhidrosis is typically spared — hence a partial, painful Horner's.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: What is the first-line imaging for suspected significant cervical spine injury in blunt trauma, and why?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: CT cervical spine — it is far more sensitive than plain radiographs and detects fractures that plain films miss. It is preferred especially in higher-risk or older patients and those with reduced GCS.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Which two clinical decision rules determine who needs cervical spine imaging?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: The Canadian C-spine rule and the NEXUS criteria. They allow low-risk patients to be cleared clinically without imaging. Image if there is a high-risk factor (age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, limb paraesthesiae) or the patient cannot actively rotate the neck 45 degrees each way.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Name the three classic upper cervical spine fractures and their mechanisms.
investigations__CT__Spine.back:
• Jefferson fracture (C1 burst, axial load, lateral mass spread on peg view)
  • Odontoid peg fracture (C2 dens; Anderson-D'Alonzo type II at the base is commonest and unstable)
  • Hangman's fracture (traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2, bilateral pars/pedicle, hyperextension).

investigations__CT__Spine.front: When is MRI added after CT cervical spine, and what does it assess?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: MRI is added to assess the spinal cord, ligaments and discs. Classic example: central cord syndrome in an elderly patient after a hyperextension injury, where CT shows no fracture but MRI reveals cord signal change.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Why must you never clinically clear the cervical spine in an obtunded or intoxicated patient, and which condition is a specific trap?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: Clinical clearance requires a reliable examination; obtunded, intoxicated or distracting-injury patients cannot be assessed, so they must be imaged. Beware ankylosing spondylitis / DISH, where trivial trauma can cause unstable transverse fractures.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Which spinal column, if involved, most strongly implies instability, and what structure defines it?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: The MIDDLE column (posterior vertebral body wall + posterior longitudinal ligament). Involvement of ≥2 columns — especially the middle column — implies an unstable injury (Denis 3-column concept).

investigations__CT__Spine.front: How does a burst fracture differ from a simple wedge compression fracture?
investigations__CT__Spine.back:
• A wedge fracture involves the ANTERIOR column only (usually stable).
  • A BURST fracture is an axial-load injury involving ANTERIOR + MIDDLE columns with RETROPULSION of bone into the canal — unstable and risks cord injury.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: A patient in an RTC has a horizontal fracture through all three columns of L2. What is the diagnosis and key association?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: A CHANCE (flexion-distraction / 'seat-belt') fracture. It mandates a search for INTRA-ABDOMINAL injuries — bowel, mesenteric and pancreatic — which are commonly associated.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Which region of the thoracolumbar spine is the commonest site of injury and why?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: The THORACOLUMBAR JUNCTION (T11–L2). It is a biomechanical transition zone between the rigid, rib-splinted thoracic spine and the mobile lumbar spine, concentrating stress.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: CT shows atraumatic vertebral collapse with bony destruction and posterior wall involvement. What must be excluded and what is the key investigation?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: A pathological (malignant) collapse — metastasis or myeloma. Do MRI whole spine to assess marrow and exclude spinal cord compression.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Which imaging modality is the investigation of choice for suspected cauda equina syndrome, and why not CT?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: Urgent MRI of the whole spine. CT poorly demonstrates the soft-tissue disc, nerve roots and cauda equina, whereas MRI shows the compressed neural elements directly. Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency needing urgent decompression.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: What is spondylolysis and its classic radiological sign?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: A defect (stress fracture) of the pars interarticularis. On oblique/CT views it produces the classic 'Scottie dog collar' (or broken neck) sign. Bilateral defects can progress to spondylolisthesis.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Describe a burst fracture on CT lumbar spine and the key thing to assess.
investigations__CT__Spine.back: Comminuted vertebral body fracture from axial loading, with retropulsion of a posterior bony fragment into the spinal canal. Key assessment is the degree of canal compromise (and associated neurological deficit).

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Give the red-flag features of cauda equina syndrome.
investigations__CT__Spine.back:
• Saddle (perineal) anaesthesia
  • bladder dysfunction (retention with overflow / incontinence)
  • bowel dysfunction and reduced anal tone
  • bilateral sciatica/radiculopathy
  • and sexual dysfunction.
It is a surgical emergency.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: How does neurogenic claudication (lumbar canal stenosis) differ clinically from vascular claudication?
investigations__CT__Spine.back:
• Neurogenic: bilateral leg pain/heaviness on walking, relieved by lumbar flexion/sitting (e.g. leaning on a trolley), and can be provoked by standing/extension.
  • Vascular: pain relieved simply by stopping/standing still, with reduced pulses.
CT/MRI shows facet arthropathy, osteophytes and canal narrowing in neurogenic claudication.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Why does finding a single spinal fracture mandate CT of the whole spine?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: Because ~10–15% of patients with one spinal fracture have a second, non-contiguous fracture at a distant level that would otherwise be missed.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Which patients cannot have their spine "cleared" clinically and therefore need imaging?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: Obtunded / reduced-GCS or intoxicated patients, and those with neurological signs or a distracting injury — they cannot be reliably examined, so they must be immobilised and imaged.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: Why is ankylosing spondylitis / DISH a red flag in spinal trauma?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: The rigid, fused spine fractures across all three columns even after trivial trauma, producing highly unstable transverse fractures that are easily missed — so have a very low threshold for whole-spine CT.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: When is MRI added after a trauma CT whole spine?
investigations__CT__Spine.back: For neurological deficit, suspected cord or ligamentous injury, SCIWORA (esp. children), and to help clear the obtunded patient's C-spine per local protocol — CT images bone, MRI images cord/soft tissue.

investigations__CT__Spine.front: How does neurogenic shock differ from haemorrhagic shock in spinal cord injury?
investigations__CT__Spine.back:
• Neurogenic shock (high cord injury, sympathetic disruption) causes hypotension WITH bradycardia
  • haemorrhagic shock causes hypotension with tachycardia.
Both may coexist — exclude bleeding.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What are the three windows every contrast CT chest should be reviewed on, and what does each show?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Lung window (parenchyma — nodules, consolidation, emphysema, bronchiectasis)
  • mediastinal/soft-tissue window (nodes, masses, vessels, pleura)
  • and bone window (mets, fractures).

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What are the anterior mediastinal "4 Ts"?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Thymoma
  • Teratoma (germ-cell tumour)
  • Thyroid (retrosternal goitre)
  • and "Terrible" lymphoma.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: On contrast CT, which pleural features suggest MALIGNANT pleural disease?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Nodular pleural thickening
  • circumferential (encasing) thickening
  • mediastinal pleural involvement
  • and thickening >1 cm.
These suggest mesothelioma (asbestos exposure) or metastatic pleural disease.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What is the "split pleura" sign and what does it indicate?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: Enhancement and thickening of both the visceral and parietal pleura separated by a loculated fluid collection — indicating an empyema.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What safety checks are needed before giving IV iodinated contrast for a CT chest?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Renal function (eGFR/AKI risk of contrast nephropathy)
  • previous contrast allergy/reaction
  • and metformin use.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: When is a non-contrast (rather than contrast-enhanced) CT chest preferred?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: When IV contrast is unnecessary or contraindicated — e.g. renal impairment or contrast allergy — and when the question is about lung parenchyma/nodules, coronary calcium or nodule follow-up, where contrast adds little.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: List the five features used to characterise a solitary pulmonary nodule on CT.
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Size
  • margins (spiculated/irregular = suspicious, smooth = benign)
  • calcification pattern
  • presence of fat (hamartoma)
  • and growth on serial scans.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: Which calcification patterns in a lung nodule suggest a benign lesion?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Central
  • laminated (concentric)
  • popcorn (hamartoma)
  • and diffuse/dense calcification.
Eccentric or absent calcification is worrying for malignancy.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What CT features make a pulmonary nodule almost certainly benign?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Small size
  • smooth margins
  • benign calcification pattern (or intralesional fat = hamartoma)
  • and stability for ≥2 years on serial imaging.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: Why must every CT chest be justified, and what dose principle applies?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: CT delivers a significant radiation dose, so scans must be justified against benefit and use the lowest appropriate protocol (ALARA). Low-dose non-contrast CT is used for nodule surveillance and screening.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What HRCT pattern supports a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: A UIP (usual interstitial pneumonia) pattern: peripheral/subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: How do you distinguish ground-glass opacification from consolidation on HRCT, and what does ground-glass imply?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: Ground-glass is hazy increased attenuation that does NOT obscure the underlying vessels/bronchial walls (consolidation does). It implies active alveolitis/inflammation or infection (e.g. PCP, HP, NSIP) and is potentially reversible/treatable.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What is the 'signet-ring sign' on HRCT and what does it indicate?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: A dilated bronchus that is wider than its accompanying pulmonary artery, seen in cross-section as a ring with the artery as the 'stone'. It indicates bronchiectasis (irreversible bronchial dilatation).

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: Give the differentials for UPPER-zone versus LOWER-zone pulmonary fibrosis.
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: Upper zone: TB, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, ankylosing spondylitis, radiation, silicosis/coal (pneumoconioses). Lower zone: IPF, asbestosis, connective tissue disease, and drugs (methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin).

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: Which drugs classically cause a lower-zone/interstitial pneumonitis or pulmonary fibrosis?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• Methotrexate
  • amiodarone
  • nitrofurantoin
  • and bleomycin.
Always take a drug history and stop the culprit if drug-induced lung disease is suspected.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What is the first-line definitive imaging test for suspected pulmonary embolism, and what is the classic finding?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA). A PE appears as a filling defect within a contrast-opacified pulmonary artery; a large clot straddling the bifurcation is a saddle embolus.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: How does the two-level Wells score direct investigation of suspected PE (NICE)?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• PE LIKELY (Wells >4) → immediate CTPA (interim anticoagulation if delayed).
  • PE UNLIKELY (Wells ≤4) → D-dimer; if raised → CTPA, if normal → PE excluded.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: When is a V/Q scan preferred over CTPA for PE?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: When CTPA is contraindicated — renal impairment, contrast allergy — or in pregnancy, a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan is the alternative.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What CTPA/echo features indicate a large, high-risk PE with right heart strain?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: RV dilatation, RV:LV ratio >1, and septal bowing toward the left ventricle; a peripheral wedge infarct may also be seen. These mark a haemodynamically significant PE.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: How is PE managed, and what changes with haemodynamic instability?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: Anticoagulation with a DOAC first-line (NICE). A massive PE with haemodynamic instability (hypotension/shock) needs thrombolysis (e.g. alteplase) or embolectomy.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What is the first-line staging investigation for confirmed or suspected lung cancer, and what anatomy must it cover?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest AND upper abdomen — extended to include the liver and adrenals (common metastatic sites). It provides TNM staging.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What is the correct lung cancer staging pathway after the initial CT?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: CT chest/abdomen → PET-CT (functional; detects occult nodal/distant disease and upstages) → tissue diagnosis (EBUS/bronchoscopy for central & nodal, CT-guided biopsy for peripheral) → MDT decides treatment. Brain needs dedicated contrast CT/MRI head.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: Why is EBUS-TBNA so important in lung cancer staging?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: It samples mediastinal lymph nodes to confirm the N stage. Mediastinal nodal involvement/invasion often makes the tumour inoperable, so accurate N staging is crucial for deciding resectability.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: On staging CT, what short-axis nodal size is regarded as pathologically enlarged, and what are the common M1 sites?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
A node >1 cm in short axis is suspicious. Common metastatic sites:
  • liver
  • adrenals
  • bone
  • contralateral lung
  • and brain (brain requires dedicated CT/MRI head).

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: Contrast the typical treatment approach for NSCLC vs SCLC.
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• NSCLC: early/operable → surgery ± adjuvant; locally advanced → chemoradiotherapy ± immunotherapy; metastatic → systemic/palliative therapy.
  • SCLC: usually disseminated at presentation → chemotherapy (limited vs extensive stage).

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: What is low-dose CT (LDCT) lung screening and who is it for in the UK?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: A reduced-radiation, non-contrast CT chest used to screen ASYMPTOMATIC high-risk people for lung cancer. In the UK it is delivered via the NHS Targeted Lung Health Check programme, inviting ever-smokers (current or ex) aged ~55–74 identified as high-risk by a validated model (e.g. PLCOm2012), with repeat LDCT at intervals and smoking cessation support.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: Which trials support LDCT lung screening and what did they show?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: NLST (US) and NELSON (Europe). Both showed LDCT screening of high-risk smokers reduces lung-cancer mortality — around a 20% relative reduction in NLST compared with the control arm.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: List the main harms of LDCT lung cancer screening.
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
• False positives (benign nodules causing anxiety and further tests/biopsy risk)
  • overdiagnosis (indolent cancers that would never have caused harm)
  • radiation exposure
  • and incidental findings requiring further investigation.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: How are screen-detected pulmonary nodules managed?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back:
By standardised protocols based on nodule size and growth:
  • small/low-risk nodules get interval surveillance LDCT to check for growth
  • larger, growing or higher-risk nodules are worked up with PET-CT and/or biopsy and referred to the lung MDT.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.front: A high-risk patient invited for lung screening reports haemoptysis and weight loss. What is the correct action?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.back: They are now symptomatic, so screening is inappropriate — refer via the urgent 2-week-wait symptomatic cancer pathway, not the routine asymptomatic screening programme.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What is the NICE first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected coronary origin?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: CT coronary angiography (CTCA). Offer it for typical or atypical angina, or for non-anginal chest pain with an abnormal resting ECG (e.g. Q waves).

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What is the main diagnostic strength of a normal CTCA?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: A very high negative predictive value — a normal CTCA effectively excludes significant obstructive coronary artery disease (it is best at ruling out CAD).

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: Beyond luminal stenosis, what else can CTCA assess?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: The vessel wall — it characterises both calcified and non-calcified (soft) plaque, and can be combined with a coronary artery calcium score for risk stratification.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What practical preparation is needed for a diagnostic CTCA?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back:
• A slow, regular heart rate (beta-blockers often given, target ~<60–65 bpm) with a reliable breath-hold
  • IV iodinated contrast (check renal function/allergy)
  • GTN may be given to dilate the coronaries.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: Is CTCA the appropriate primary test for suspected acute coronary syndrome?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: No. ACS is investigated with ECG and troponin via the ACS pathway (primary PCI for STEMI). CTCA is for STABLE chest pain, not acute presentations.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What is the coronary artery calcium (CAC) score and how is it acquired?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: A non-contrast, ECG-gated CT that quantifies calcified atherosclerotic plaque in the coronary arteries using the Agatston score. It is low-dose and reflects total atherosclerotic plaque burden.

• 0 = no calcified plaque (very low event risk)
  • 1–99 = mild
  • 100–399 = moderate
  • ≥400 = extensive calcification / high risk.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What is the significance of a calcium score of 0?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: No identifiable calcified plaque, indicating very low risk of a coronary event — it has a strong negative predictive value for events.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What are the main clinical uses of coronary calcium scoring?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back:
• Reported alongside/derived from CTCA in stable chest pain assessment
  • and to refine cardiovascular risk in selected asymptomatic/intermediate-risk people to guide statin decisions when risk is uncertain.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What is the key limitation of the calcium score?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: It detects calcified plaque only. Soft (non-calcified) plaque can cause stenosis with a low/zero score, and a high score does not prove obstructive stenosis — lumen assessment needs CTCA or functional testing. It is not a test for acute chest pain.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What is the definitive investigation for acute aortic syndromes and aortic aneurysm?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back:
CT angiography of the aorta (CT aortogram) — arterial-phase IV contrast. It diagnoses
  • dissection
  • aneurysm ± rupture
  • traumatic aortic injury
  • intramural haematoma
  • and penetrating aortic ulcer.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: Describe the Stanford classification of aortic dissection and its management.
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back:
• Type A involves the ascending aorta (± arch/descending) and is a surgical emergency (risk of tamponade, aortic regurgitation, coronary/cerebral malperfusion).
  • Type B is descending only (distal to left subclavian) and is usually managed medically with strict BP/HR control (e.g. IV labetalol) unless complicated.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: What are the CT features of an aortic dissection?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: An intimal flap separating a true lumen from a false lumen; the false lumen arises from an intimal tear and typically fills/opacifies more slowly than the true lumen.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: When should an unstable patient with a suspected ruptured AAA NOT have a CT aortogram?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back: When they are haemodynamically unstable with a known/suspected ruptured AAA — they go straight to theatre. Do not delay for imaging. Only a stable patient gets an urgent CT aortogram to confirm and plan (EVAR vs open).

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.front: Define AAA, the threshold for elective repair, and the UK screening programme.
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.back:
• AAA = infrarenal aorta ≥3 cm.
  • Elective repair usually considered around 5.5 cm, or if rapidly growing/symptomatic.
  • UK screening: a one-off abdominal ultrasound for men at age 65.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: At what timing is the portal venous phase CT abdomen/pelvis acquired, and why is it the workhorse for the acute abdomen?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: ~60–70 s after IV contrast. At this point the liver parenchyma, bowel wall and abdominal veins all enhance optimally, so one scan interrogates solid organs, bowel viability and vasculature — ideal for the undifferentiated acute abdomen.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: List the CT features of acute appendicitis on portal venous CT.
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Dilated appendix >6 mm
  • non-compressible
  • wall thickening and enhancement
  • periappendiceal fat stranding
  • and an appendicolith (± free fluid or abscess if perforated).

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What does free intraperitoneal air on CT mean, and where/how do you look for it?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Pneumoperitoneum = perforation until proven otherwise. Look under the diaphragm and in the non-dependent (anterior) abdomen, best seen on lung/bone windows.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: Name the CT signs of bowel ischaemia.
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Bowel-wall non-enhancement
  • pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas)
  • portal venous gas
  • and mesenteric artery/vein occlusion (± bowel dilatation and mesenteric fat stranding).

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: On CT, what is the key sign that localises the cause of bowel obstruction, and what dangerous variant must you exclude?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: The transition point between dilated (small bowel >3 cm) and collapsed loops localises the cause. Exclude a closed-loop obstruction/volvulus and signs of ischaemia, which are surgical emergencies.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What is the first-line, gold-standard imaging for suspected ureteric colic, and why is it non-contrast?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: CT KUB (non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder). Nearly all urinary stones are radio-opaque and appear as bright, very high-density foci on CT; contrast is omitted because it would opacify the collecting system and obscure the stone. It is also safe in renal impairment.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: On a non-contrast CT, how does acute haemorrhage appear and roughly what are its Hounsfield units?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Acute/fresh blood is hyperdense (bright), typically around 45–70 HU — brighter than simple fluid (~0 HU). Free hyperdense fluid indicates haemoperitoneum; a hyperdense collection suggests haematoma.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: Why might a non-contrast (pre-contrast) baseline series be included in a multiphase CT?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: To measure true density before contrast — e.g. identifying a lipid-rich adrenal adenoma (≤10 HU), intralesional fat in an angiomyolipoma, or pre-existing calcification/haemorrhage — so that enhancement on later phases can be calculated and lesions characterised.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: Give two situations where non-contrast CT abdomen/pelvis is preferred specifically because contrast is contraindicated.
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Significant renal impairment (avoids contrast nephrotoxicity)
  • and previous severe iodinated-contrast allergy.
It also avoids the delay/cost of contrast when the question is only about stones, calcification or acute blood.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What key pathologies are POORLY assessed on non-contrast CT, prompting the addition of contrast?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Solid-organ lesions (need enhancement pattern)
  • bowel-wall enhancement/ischaemia
  • abscess vs phlegmon (rim enhancement)
  • and vascular pathology such as dissection, embolus or active extravasation.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: Name the three phases of a triple-phase liver CT and their approximate timings after IV contrast.
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Arterial (~25–35s)
  • portal venous (~60–70s)
  • and delayed (~3–10 min).
The dual blood supply (~75% portal, ~25% arterial) means hypervascular lesions stand out on the arterial phase.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What is the essentially diagnostic multiphase CT signature of hepatocellular carcinoma in a cirrhotic liver?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Arterial-phase hyperenhancement (wash-IN) followed by portal/delayed washout (becoming hypodense relative to liver) ± an enhancing capsule. AFP may be raised; no biopsy is needed to diagnose in this setting.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: How does a hepatic haemangioma enhance on multiphase CT?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with progressive centripetal 'fill-in' on delayed phases, following the blood pool. It is the commonest benign liver lesion.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: On which phase are hypovascular metastases (e.g. colorectal) best seen, and why?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Portal venous phase — the background liver parenchyma enhances maximally, so hypovascular metastases appear darkest (hypodense) against it. Some metastases are hypervascular (neuroendocrine, RCC, melanoma, thyroid) and are seen on arterial phase.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What imaging feature distinguishes focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) from other arterially hyperenhancing lesions?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: A central scar that classically enhances on the delayed phase, in a lesion showing arterial hyperenhancement.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: Which two phases make up a pancreatic-protocol CT, and why?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: A pancreatic (late arterial, ~40s) phase — pancreas enhances so a hypodense tumour and arterial anatomy (SMA/coeliac) stand out — and a portal venous (~70s) phase — best for liver metastases, nodes and the SMV/portal vein.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What is the 'double duct sign' and what does it suggest?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Simultaneous dilatation of the common bile duct AND the pancreatic duct, typically from an obstructing pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. Presents as painless obstructive jaundice.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: On CT, how is resectability of pancreatic adenocarcinoma judged?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: By vascular involvement: contact/encasement of the SMA, coeliac axis or SMV/portal vein. >180 degrees of contact (encasement) usually means locally advanced/unresectable; also look for liver/peritoneal metastases and distant nodes. Resectable head lesions may have a Whipple's.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: When should CT be performed in acute pancreatitis, and why not earlier?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: At around 72h or later, to assess severity and complications (necrosis, collections). Diagnosis is clinical + amylase/lipase; early CT can look falsely normal as necrosis has not yet declared itself.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What CT finding indicates infected pancreatic necrosis?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Gas (locules) within a peripancreatic/necrotic collection. This is life-threatening, needs specialist input and often intervention (e.g. drainage/necrosectomy).

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What is the first-line imaging investigation for visible (frank) haematuria in an adult, and what test must accompany it?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: CT urogram (CTU) to assess the upper tract for renal and urothelial tumours, PLUS flexible cystoscopy to assess the bladder (the commonest cause). CTU does not replace cystoscopy.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: Name the three main phases of a CT urogram and what each detects.
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Non-contrast (calculi and calcification)
  • nephrographic (enhancing renal parenchymal masses / RCC)
  • and delayed excretory (contrast opacifies collecting system and ureters — filling defects and strictures).

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: On the excretory phase of a CTU, a filling defect within the opacified ureter or collecting system suggests what?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: An upper-tract urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma until proven otherwise. Differentials include a non-opaque (radiolucent) stone or blood clot — correlate with the non-contrast phase.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: State the NICE 2-week-wait referral criteria for suspected urological (bladder) cancer.
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Visible haematuria in adults aged ≥45 (unexplained, or persisting/recurring after treatment of UTI)
  • OR aged ≥60 with unexplained non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or a raised WCC.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What are the main disadvantages of CT urography compared with single-phase CT?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• A significant iodinated contrast load (caution in renal impairment / eGFR)
  • and a higher cumulative radiation dose because of the multiple acquisition phases.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What is the first-line / gold-standard investigation for suspected renal (ureteric) colic, and within what timeframe does NICE recommend it?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: Urgent low-dose NON-CONTRAST CT KUB, ideally within 24 hours. It detects almost all calculi, including radiolucent uric acid stones invisible on plain film (only rare indinavir stones are CT-occult).

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What are the three anatomical narrowings where ureteric stones impact, and which is commonest?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: 1) Pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ), 2) where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim/iliac vessels, 3) vesico-ureteric junction (VUJ) — the VUJ is the narrowest point and the commonest site of impaction.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: Besides the stone itself, what secondary CT signs confirm significant ureteric obstruction?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• Hydronephrosis and hydroureter
  • perinephric fat stranding
  • and ureteric wall oedema (the 'soft-tissue rim sign', which helps distinguish a stone from a phlebolith).

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: How does stone size guide the likelihood of spontaneous passage and management?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back:
• <5 mm usually pass spontaneously (conservative).
  • 5–10 mm may pass — medical expulsive therapy with an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) for distal stones.
  • >10 mm rarely pass and need intervention (ESWL, ureteroscopy, or PCNL for large/staghorn stones).

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: What is the urological emergency associated with a ureteric stone, and how is it managed?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: An obstructed, infected kidney (obstructing stone + fever/sepsis or pyonephrosis). Manage with IV antibiotics and URGENT decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent). Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a single/transplant kidney also needs urgent decompression due to AKI.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.front: First-line analgesia for renal colic?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.back: An NSAID (e.g. PR diclofenac), plus antiemetics and fluids.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What is the investigation of choice for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: CT mesenteric angiography (arterial-phase CT). It demonstrates the arterial filling defect/occlusion and late signs of bowel ischaemia (non-enhancement, pneumatosis, portal venous gas).

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What is the commonest cause of acute mesenteric ischaemia and its typical source?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: SMA embolus — most commonly from a cardiac source, classically atrial fibrillation.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: Name three late CT signs of established bowel infarction in mesenteric ischaemia.
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back:
• Bowel-wall non-enhancement
  • pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall)
  • and portal venous gas.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What CT finding localises an acute GI bleed on angiography, and what does it require?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: Active contrast extravasation into the bowel lumen (a "blush"). It requires a brisk/active bleeding rate to be positive and guides embolisation or surgery.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: Give the classic triad suggesting acute mesenteric ischaemia.
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back:
• Sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings
  • atrial fibrillation or vascular disease
  • and a raised lactate with metabolic acidosis.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What two bowel preparations are required before CT colonography, and why?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back:
• Oral bowel prep (often with faecal tagging) to clear/label stool
  • and colonic insufflation with CO₂ via a rectal catheter to distend the colon.
Distension and clean bowel allow polyps and cancers to be seen; scanning is done supine and prone to shift residual fluid/stool.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: Give three situations where CT colonography is preferred over colonoscopy.
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back:
• Frail/elderly patients (avoids sedation)
  • incomplete colonoscopy (e.g. obstructing tumour or tortuous colon)
  • and patients who cannot tolerate or decline colonoscopy.
Also to assess the proximal colon beyond an obstructing distal cancer.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What is the classic CTC appearance of a colorectal carcinoma?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: A short annular, constricting "apple-core" lesion with shouldered margins and luminal narrowing, or a polypoid intraluminal mass. Polyps appear as filling defects/wall protrusions.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What is the key limitation of CTC compared with colonoscopy?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: CTC is purely diagnostic — it cannot biopsy or remove lesions. Any suspicious lesion still requires colonoscopy for tissue diagnosis and polypectomy.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: When is CT colonography relatively contraindicated?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: In acute severe colitis or where perforation risk is high, because colonic insufflation can perforate inflamed or weakened bowel. Recent perforation risk is also a contraindication.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: How does CTC fit into UK bowel-cancer screening and red-flag pathways?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: Screening is via FIT (faecal immunochemical test) leading to colonoscopy, with CTC used where colonoscopy is unsuitable. Red-flag symptoms (change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass) trigger a 2-week-wait referral.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What is the purpose of the oral contrast in CT enterography, and what type is used?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: A large volume of NEUTRAL (low-density) oral contrast — water or a mannitol-type agent — is drunk to DISTEND the small bowel. Combined with IV contrast, this makes mural thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement clearly visible against the low-density lumen.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: What is the 'comb sign' on CT enterography and what does it indicate?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: Engorged vasa recta (mesenteric hypervascularity) arranged like the teeth of a comb along an affected bowel segment — a sign of ACTIVE Crohn's inflammation.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: List key CT enterography findings of active Crohn's disease.
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back:
• Mural thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement
  • comb sign
  • fibrofatty proliferation ('creeping fat')
  • skip lesions with terminal-ileal involvement;
complications include strictures (with pre-stenotic dilatation), fistulae, sinus tracts and abscesses.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: Why does distinguishing active from fibrotic disease on CTE matter?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: Active inflammatory disease (enhancing, oedematous wall) is managed MEDICALLY, whereas fibrotic stricturing (fixed narrowing, non-enhancing) often needs SURGERY or endoscopic dilatation — so the distinction guides treatment.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: When is MRI enterography preferred over CT enterography?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: In younger patients and for repeated follow-up, because it avoids ionising radiation. CT enterography is quicker/more available and better in the acute setting.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: On an adrenal washout CT, what non-contrast attenuation value confirms a benign lipid-rich adenoma and requires no further characterisation?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: Low attenuation ≤10 HU on the non-contrast phase = lipid-rich adenoma (benign). No washout calculation or further imaging is needed.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: For a lipid-poor adrenal lesion (>10 HU), what washout thresholds indicate a benign adenoma?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: Absolute washout ≥60% or relative washout ≥40% indicates a benign adenoma. Low/poor washout suggests a non-adenoma (metastasis, phaeochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma).

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: Which biochemical tests make up the functional screen for every adrenal incidentaloma?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back:
• Plasma/urinary metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma)
  • overnight dexamethasone suppression test (Cushing's)
  • and aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn's/primary hyperaldosteronism, especially with hypertension or hypokalaemia).

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: Why must phaeochromocytoma be excluded before biopsy of an adrenal mass?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back: Biopsy or manipulation of an unblocked phaeochromocytoma can trigger catastrophic catecholamine release and a life-threatening hypertensive crisis. Exclude it biochemically (metanephrines) first.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.front: List the CT morphological features of an adrenal mass that raise concern for malignancy.
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.back:
• Large size (>4 cm)
  • irregular margins
  • heterogeneity/necrosis
  • and rapid growth on serial imaging
— suggesting adrenocortical carcinoma or metastasis (adrenals are a common metastatic site for lung and breast).

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: Why is CT preferred over plain X-ray for complex upper limb fractures?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: CT provides high-resolution bony detail with multiplanar and 3D reconstructions, showing the number and position of fragments, articular step, comminution and displacement — essential for surgical planning of intra-articular fractures where plain films are insufficient.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: A patient has anatomical snuffbox tenderness but a normal initial wrist X-ray. What is the management?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Treat as a clinical scaphoid fracture: immobilise (e.g. wrist splint/cast) and re-image with CT or MRI to detect an occult scaphoid fracture. Do not dismiss on the basis of a normal X-ray.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: Why do proximal pole scaphoid fractures carry a high risk of AVN and non-union?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply entering distally, so a proximal pole fracture disrupts perfusion to the proximal fragment, predisposing to avascular necrosis and non-union.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: Name upper limb fractures where CT is commonly used for characterisation and surgical planning.
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back:
• Occult scaphoid fracture
  • complex/intra-articular distal radius fractures
  • radial head and complex intra-articular distal humerus (including terrible triad)
  • and scapula/glenoid fractures;
also assessment of union/non-union and hardware position.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: What upper limb fracture situations are surgical emergencies requiring urgent orthopaedic input?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: An open fracture, or any fracture with neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome — all require urgent orthopaedic assessment and intervention.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: Why is CT preferred over plain films for complex lower-limb fractures?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Plain films underestimate the injury. CT depicts articular step-off, depression, comminution and fragment position in 3D, which is essential for planning internal fixation of intra-articular fractures.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: Which classification does CT refine for tibial plateau fractures, and what complication must be watched for in high-energy cases?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: The Schatzker classification. High-energy tibial plateau (and shaft) fractures risk acute compartment syndrome.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: What is Böhler's angle and how does it change in a calcaneal fracture?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: An angle measured on the lateral hindfoot between lines along the posterior facet and the anterior process of the calcaneus. It is reduced/flattened in calcaneal fractures.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: A patient has a calcaneal fracture after a fall from height. What associated injury must you actively exclude?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Associated axial/spinal fractures (e.g. lumbar spine) — calcaneal fractures from axial load are commonly bilateral and linked to spinal injury; image the spine.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: Give the key clinical features of acute compartment syndrome and the required management.
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back:
• Severe pain out of proportion
  • pain on passive stretch
  • and a tense compartment.
Treatment is urgent fasciotomy. Do not wait for pulselessness, which is a late sign.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: Why does a pelvic ring fracture usually involve two sites?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: The pelvis is a closed ring, so it is mechanically difficult to break in only one place — a single visible fracture should prompt a search for a second break or ligamentous disruption (commonly in the posterior ring: sacrum or SI joint), which CT detects far better than plain films.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: What defines an APC ("open-book") pelvic injury and why is it dangerous?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Anteroposterior compression springs the ring open, producing pubic symphysis diastasis and sacroiliac joint disruption. This massively increases pelvic volume and can cause catastrophic venous and arterial haemorrhage.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: What does CT (with 3D) add in acetabular fractures?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Acetabular fractures are intra-articular; CT with 3D reconstruction defines anterior/posterior column and anterior/posterior wall involvement (Judet-Letournel), guiding the surgical approach and fixation to restore joint congruity.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: How does CT angiography change management of a bleeding pelvis?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Arterial-phase CT can show a contrast blush (active arterial extravasation), identifying a patient for angio-embolisation. Note much pelvic bleeding is venous/bony and is controlled by binder tamponade rather than embolisation.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: A trauma patient with a pelvic fracture has blood at the urethral meatus — what must you avoid, and what next?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Suspected urethral injury — do NOT insert a urethral catheter until injury is excluded with a retrograde urethrogram. Also assess for high-riding prostate and perineal/scrotal bruising.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: What is a CT peripheral angiogram (“run-off”) and what does it image?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: A timed IV-contrast CT that images the arterial tree from the aorta through the iliacs and down the legs to the feet, mapping stenoses, occlusions and collaterals to localise disease and plan revascularisation (angioplasty/stent vs bypass).

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: What ABPI values indicate PAD, and what causes a falsely elevated ABPI?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: ABPI <0.9 = PAD (very low = critical ischaemia). ABPI >1.3 may be falsely elevated due to calcified, incompressible vessels, classically in diabetes — use toe-brachial index or imaging instead.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: List the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia and note which two are most sinister.
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back:
• Pain
  • Pallor
  • Pulselessness
  • Perishingly cold
  • Paraesthesia
  • Paralysis.
Paraesthesia and paralysis indicate a threatened or irreversible limb and demand emergency revascularisation.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: How does critical limb ischaemia present, and how is it distinguished from claudication?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Claudication = calf pain on walking, relieved by rest. Critical limb ischaemia = rest pain (worse at night, relieved by hanging foot out of bed), ulceration and gangrene — a limb-threatening state needing urgent revascularisation.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.front: How does CT run-off findings guide choice between endovascular and surgical treatment in PAD?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.back: Short focal stenoses favour endovascular angioplasty/stenting; long occlusions or multilevel disease favour surgical bypass. It localises disease to aortoiliac, femoropopliteal or infrapopliteal segments.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: What is the prerequisite for sending a major-trauma patient for a whole-body pan-scan CT?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: The patient must be haemodynamically stable enough (or a transient responder to resuscitation) after the ATLS primary survey. A persistently unstable patient goes to theatre or interventional radiology for haemorrhage control, NOT the scanner.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Outline the standard trauma pan-scan protocol.
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: Non-contrast head and cervical spine, followed by contrast-enhanced chest/abdomen/pelvis — often dual-phase abdomen (arterial phase for active arterial bleeding/vascular injury, portal-venous phase for solid-organ parenchyma and free fluid), with an optional delayed phase for the collecting system/bladder.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: What does an arterial-phase contrast 'blush' within a solid organ signify, and why does it matter?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: It represents active contrast extravasation, i.e. ongoing arterial bleeding. It upgrades management towards angioembolisation (IR) or surgery rather than conservative observation.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Name the key life-threatening injuries the pan-scan is systematically searched for.
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back:
• Intracranial haemorrhage
  • cervical spine fracture
  • aortic injury (isthmus/mediastinal haematoma)
  • haemo/pneumothorax
  • solid-organ injury with active extravasation
  • unstable pelvic fracture
  • and free intraperitoneal fluid (possible hollow-viscus/mesenteric injury).

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: What does the evidence show about pan-scan vs selective CT in trauma?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: Immediate total-body (pan-scan) CT did not reduce overall mortality compared with selective CT, though it reached a complete diagnosis faster. Selective scanning is favoured to limit radiation, especially in low-energy mechanisms, reliable examinations, and children/young adults.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: What does each letter of TNM staging represent, and which one most often converts curative intent to palliative?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back:
• T = size/local extent of the primary tumour
  • N = regional nodal involvement
  • M = distant metastasis.
Finding M1 (distant metastasis) on staging CT typically shifts management from curative/resectable to systemic or palliative treatment.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Why is staging CT of the abdomen acquired in the portal-venous phase (~60–70 s)?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: In the portal-venous phase the liver parenchyma enhances maximally, so hypovascular metastases stay relatively hypodense and stand out; bowel wall, spleen and lymph nodes are also well opacified, maximising detection of nodal and visceral disease.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: List the common metastatic patterns a radiologist checks on a staging CT CAP.
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back:
• Lung nodules (haematogenous)
  • liver deposits (hypodense in portal-venous phase)
  • adrenal metastases (esp. lung cancer)
  • bone deposits (lytic/sclerotic on bone windows)
  • peritoneal disease (omental caking/ascites)
  • and lymphadenopathy (enlarged/rounded nodes along drainage pathways).

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: What is RECIST and how is it used with staging/follow-up CT?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: RECIST is a standardised framework for assessing treatment response. A limited number of target lesions are measured by longest diameter at baseline and remeasured on follow-up CT; the summed change classifies response as complete/partial response, stable disease, or progression.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: When do you reach for PET-CT or MRI rather than relying on CT alone for staging?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: CT is the anatomical workhorse. PET-CT adds metabolic (FDG) information — better for occult nodal/distant disease and characterising indeterminate lesions (e.g. lung cancer, lymphoma). MRI gives superior soft-tissue contrast for local staging of rectal, prostate, liver and brain disease.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Why does 18F-FDG accumulate in metabolically active cells?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: FDG is a glucose analogue taken up via GLUT transporters and phosphorylated by hexokinase to FDG-6-phosphate, which cannot continue through glycolysis and is metabolically trapped. Glucose-avid cells (many cancers, infection, inflammation) accumulate tracer and appear as hot spots.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: What does SUV measure on PET-CT?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: Standardised Uptake Value — a semi-quantitative index of tracer uptake normalised to injected dose and body weight (SUVmax for the hottest voxel). Used to compare lesions and track treatment response, but influenced by blood glucose, uptake time and technique.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Give examples of physiological FDG uptake that can mimic or mask disease.
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back:
• Brain (obligate glucose use)
  • myocardium
  • brown fat (often supraclavicular)
  • bowel
  • and the urinary tract due to renal excretion (kidneys, ureters, bladder).

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Why must blood glucose be controlled before an FDG PET-CT?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: Hyperglycaemia means endogenous glucose competes with FDG for uptake, reducing tumour avidity and risking false-negative results. Patients fast ~6 hours and glucose is checked/optimised before injection.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Name tumour types prone to false-negative FDG PET-CT.
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back:
• Low-grade / indolent tumours
  • mucinous adenocarcinomas
  • and lesions smaller than about 1 cm (below scanner spatial resolution)
may be non-avid and missed.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Core-needle biopsy vs FNA — key difference and when core is essential?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: Core-needle biopsy gives a tissue core that preserves architecture (needed for lymphoma subtyping, tumour grading, immunohistochemistry); FNA gives cells for cytology only. Prefer core when histological architecture/IHC is required.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Most common significant complication of CT-guided LUNG biopsy, and the mandatory post-procedure test?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: Pneumothorax. Perform an erect chest X-ray after the procedure (e.g. ~1 hour later) to exclude a delayed pneumothorax before discharge; a large or symptomatic one may need a chest drain.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: Which coagulation checks are mandatory before percutaneous CT-guided biopsy?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: Platelet count and INR/clotting. Stop/withhold antiplatelets (e.g. clopidogrel) and anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs) beforehand and correct any derangement — never biopsy blind, as uncorrected coagulopathy risks catastrophic haemorrhage.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: What is CT-guided drainage and how is the catheter placed?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back: CT-guided percutaneous drainage places a catheter into an abscess or fluid collection for diagnosis and treatment, using the Seldinger technique (needle, guidewire, then railroaded drain), path planned to avoid bowel and vessels.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.front: List the main complications to counsel for before CT-guided biopsy.
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.back:
• Bleeding/haemorrhage
  • pneumothorax (esp. lung biopsy)
  • infection
  • pain
