  • and the rare risk of tumour seeding along the needle track.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 24-year-old man is struck on the side of the head with a cricket ball. He briefly loses consciousness, recovers and talks normally, then 45 minutes later becomes drowsy. Non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense biconvex collection over the left temporal region that does not cross the suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: A biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense collection that does not cross sutures, with a lucid interval after temporal trauma, is a classic arterial extradural haematoma from the middle meningeal artery. A subdural would be crescent-shaped and cross sutures; a chronic bleed would be hypodense (dark).

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: An 82-year-old woman on warfarin presents with gradual confusion over two weeks after a minor fall. Non-contrast CT shows a hypodense crescent-shaped collection over the right cerebral convexity crossing the suture lines. Which single feature best explains why this collection appears DARK rather than bright?
options: It contains mostly CSF from a torn arachnoid
The bleed is chronic, so blood has become hypodense over time
She was scanned with intravenous contrast
It is an area of acute infarction rather than blood
The collection is actually fat within a dermoid
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: The bleed is chronic, so blood has become hypodense over time
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: Crescent shape crossing sutures indicates a subdural haematoma. Acute blood is hyperdense but becomes isodense at ~1 week and hypodense/dark when chronic. The two-week history in an anticoagulated elderly patient fits a chronic subdural, explaining the dark appearance.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 55-year-old woman has a sudden 'worst-ever' occipital headache. Non-contrast CT performed 10 hours later is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as CT has excluded serious pathology
Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours from onset to look for xanthochromia
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours from onset to look for xanthochromia
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: A normal CT does not exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage. With persisting clinical suspicion, proceed to lumbar puncture, timed at least 12 hours from headache onset, to allow xanthochromia (bilirubin breakdown) to develop and be detected. Thrombolysis is contraindicated and reassurance/discharge is unsafe.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 58-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of worsening headache and progressive left-sided weakness. Contrast-enhanced CT head shows a single mass in the right frontal lobe with a thick, irregular enhancing rim, central necrosis and surrounding low density, extending across the midline through the corpus callosum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: A thick, irregular, nodular ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis that crosses the midline via the corpus callosum is the classic "butterfly" glioblastoma. An abscess gives a thin smooth ring, a meningioma is extra-axial with homogeneous enhancement, an acute lacunar infarct does not enhance in this way, and a chronic subdural is a crescentic extra-axial collection.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 34-year-old man with poorly controlled HIV (CD4 40) develops headache and confusion. He is febrile. Contrast CT head shows a solitary lesion with a thin, smooth enhancing ring and marked surrounding oedema; MRI shows central restricted diffusion. Which is the single most important immediate management step?
options: Urgent lumbar puncture before any treatment
Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and refer to neurosurgery
Commence high-dose oral corticosteroids alone and observe
Arrange outpatient MRI in two weeks
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and refer to neurosurgery
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: A thin, smooth ring with central restricted diffusion plus fever strongly suggests a cerebral abscess, which requires urgent empirical antimicrobials and neurosurgical involvement for drainage/biopsy. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with a mass lesion and oedema (herniation risk). Steroids alone or delay are unsafe. (Toxoplasmosis is a key differential in HIV, but urgent treatment and neurosurgical input remain the priority.)

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: Before performing a contrast-enhanced CT head in a 70-year-old woman with a suspected brain metastasis, which single factor most needs to be checked to reduce the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: Contrast-induced nephropathy is the key renal hazard of IV iodinated contrast, so baseline renal function (eGFR/U&E) must be checked and the patient hydrated. Allergy history and metformin status are also relevant, but of the options listed renal function is the critical one; potassium, glucose, FBC and clotting are not the primary determinants of contrast nephropathy risk.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 68-year-old man presents 90 minutes after sudden onset right-sided weakness and expressive dysphasia. An immediate non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage but a hyperdense left MCA and early loss of grey-white differentiation in the left insula. What is the single most important reason the non-contrast CT was performed first?
options: To measure the ASPECTS score for prognosis
To exclude intracranial haemorrhage before considering thrombolysis
To identify a large vessel occlusion for thrombectomy
To assess for carotid artery stenosis
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: To exclude intracranial haemorrhage before considering thrombolysis
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: The first job of the NCCT is to exclude blood, because haemorrhage absolutely contraindicates thrombolysis and management of the two stroke types diverges completely. LVO detection needs CTA, and penumbra estimation needs CTP; ASPECTS and carotid assessment are secondary to the blood-or-no-blood question.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 72-year-old woman is brought in 5 hours after sudden dense left hemiplegia and gaze deviation. NCCT excludes haemorrhage with a small early ischaemic core; CTA shows a proximal right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion demonstrates a small core with a large surrounding penumbra. Which management is most appropriate?
options: IV alteplase alone as she is within 4.5 hours
No reperfusion therapy as she is outside the thrombolysis window
Mechanical thrombectomy, as there is an LVO with favourable perfusion mismatch
Aspirin 300 mg and admit for observation only
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: Mechanical thrombectomy, as there is an LVO with favourable perfusion mismatch
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: She is beyond the 4.5h thrombolysis window, but a large vessel (M1) occlusion with a small core and large salvageable penumbra on CT perfusion identifies her for mechanical thrombectomy in the extended window (up to ~24h with favourable imaging). Aspirin alone or observation would waste salvageable brain; decompression is not indicated at this stage.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 60-year-old man on warfarin presents with sudden severe headache and reduced consciousness. Non-contrast CT shows a large hyperdense (bright) lesion in the right basal ganglia with surrounding oedema. Which is the most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Reverse anticoagulation and control blood pressure with urgent neurosurgical review
Perform CT perfusion to assess the penumbra before treatment
Give IV alteplase only if within 4.5 hours of onset
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: Reverse anticoagulation and control blood pressure with urgent neurosurgical review
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: The CT shows an intracerebral haemorrhage (hyperdense on NCCT). Thrombolysis and thrombectomy are for ischaemic stroke and are contraindicated here. Management is reversal of anticoagulation, blood pressure control and urgent neurosurgical review. CT perfusion has no role in acute haemorrhage.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 52-year-old woman presents with a sudden 'worst-ever' occipital headache and neck stiffness. A non-contrast CT head performed 4 hours later confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide definitive management?
options: CT angiogram of the Circle of Willis
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: CT angiogram of the Circle of Willis
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: Once SAH is confirmed on non-contrast CT, the next step is vascular imaging (CTA, or DSA) to localise and characterise the underlying aneurysm so it can be secured by coiling or clipping. LP for xanthochromia is only needed when the CT is negative but suspicion remains. MRI and carotid Doppler do not guide aneurysm treatment, and delaying imaging risks re-bleeding.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 60-year-old man develops acute-onset diplopia and ptosis. On examination the right eye is 'down and out' with a fixed dilated pupil, and he reports a severe headache behind that eye. Which single diagnosis must be excluded most urgently?
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: A painful third nerve palsy with pupillary involvement (fixed dilated pupil) is a compressive 'surgical' third — classically a PCom aneurysm pressing on the superficial pupillomotor fibres — and may herald rupture. A diabetic third nerve palsy characteristically spares the pupil. This requires urgent CTA/DSA and neurosurgical referral. Myasthenia and Horner syndrome do not cause a fixed dilated pupil in this pattern.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 45-year-old woman has a thunderclap headache. Non-contrast CT head at 3 hours is reported as normal, but the clinical suspicion of subarachnoid haemorrhage remains high. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate CT angiogram of the Circle of Willis
Lumbar puncture at ≥12 hours from headache onset, looking for xanthochromia
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: Lumbar puncture at ≥12 hours from headache onset, looking for xanthochromia
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: CT sensitivity for SAH falls with time, so a negative early CT does not exclude it when suspicion is high. LP performed at ≥12 hours allows time for red-cell breakdown to produce xanthochromia (detected by spectrophotometry), distinguishing true SAH from a traumatic tap. Discharge would be unsafe; CTA is reserved for once SAH is confirmed; nimodipine is treatment for confirmed aneurysmal SAH.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 26-year-old woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill presents with 5 days of worsening headache and a seizure. Non-contrast CT shows a right frontoparietal haemorrhage that does not conform to an arterial territory, with a hyperdense superior sagittal sinus. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
options: CT angiography of the intracranial arteries
CT venography of the intracranial venous sinuses
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: CT venography of the intracranial venous sinuses
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: The clinical picture (young woman on COCP, seizure, haemorrhage crossing arterial territories, hyperdense sinus) is classic cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. CTV (or MRV) opacifies the venous sinuses and demonstrates the filling defect / empty delta sign. CT angiography images arteries, not the venous system.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 34-year-old woman with confirmed superior sagittal sinus thrombosis has a small associated haemorrhagic venous infarct on CT. She is neurologically stable. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Withhold all anticoagulation because of the haemorrhage
Immediate surgical evacuation of the haematoma
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: CVST is treated with anticoagulation even when there is an associated venous haemorrhage, because the thrombus otherwise propagates and worsens venous congestion. LMWH followed by oral anticoagulation is standard; antiplatelets and antifibrinolytics are not the treatment, and surgery is not first-line.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: On a contrast-enhanced CT venogram, which finding is most specific for thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus?
options: Empty delta sign — peripheral contrast around a central filling defect
Loss of grey-white differentiation in the MCA territory
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: Empty delta sign — peripheral contrast around a central filling defect
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: The empty delta sign is enhancing contrast surrounding a central non-enhancing clot in the superior sagittal sinus and is the classic CTV finding of CVST. A hyperdense MCA and loss of grey-white differentiation indicate arterial (MCA) infarction, not venous sinus thrombosis.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A 68-year-old is found with a dense right hemiparesis on waking; last seen well 9 hours earlier. NCCT shows no haemorrhage and CTA confirms a left M1 occlusion. CT perfusion shows a 12 mL region of markedly reduced CBF and CBV, surrounded by a large 90 mL area of prolonged Tmax with preserved CBV. What does this perfusion pattern indicate?
options: A large infarct core with no salvageable tissue
A small core with a large penumbra (favourable mismatch) suitable for thrombectomy
Global hypoperfusion suggesting a haemodynamic rather than embolic cause
A matched defect indicating completed infarction of the whole territory
Contrast artefact making the study non-diagnostic
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: A small core with a large penumbra (favourable mismatch) suitable for thrombectomy
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: The small matched CBF/CBV defect is the core (12 mL), and the large surrounding Tmax delay with preserved CBV is salvageable penumbra. This favourable mismatch in a wake-up/late-window stroke selects the patient for mechanical thrombectomy in the late window (up to ~24h). A large penumbra:core ratio is the target.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: Which single statement best distinguishes salvageable penumbra from irreversibly infarcted core on CT perfusion?
options: Penumbra shows reduced CBV whereas core shows preserved CBV
Core shows prolonged Tmax whereas penumbra shows normal Tmax
Penumbra shows prolonged MTT/Tmax with preserved CBV, while core shows reduced CBF AND reduced CBV
Both show identical maps and are separated only by clinical severity
Core shows increased CBF due to luxury perfusion
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: Penumbra shows prolonged MTT/Tmax with preserved CBV, while core shows reduced CBF AND reduced CBV
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: The defining difference is blood volume. In the penumbra autoregulation maintains CBV despite delayed transit (raised MTT/Tmax), so it remains viable. In the core CBV has fallen along with CBF (a matched defect), indicating irreversible infarction. The CBV/perfusion mismatch is what identifies salvageable tissue.

investigations__CT__Head / Brain.question: A patient presents 18 hours after stroke onset. CT perfusion shows a large 85 mL core of matched CBF and CBV reduction with only a small rim of penumbra. NCCT confirms no haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate interpretation regarding reperfusion?
options: Proceed urgently to thrombectomy as the late window mandates intervention
The large core predicts poor benefit and higher haemorrhagic transformation risk, arguing against reperfusion
Give intravenous thrombolysis alone since thrombectomy is contraindicated after 6 hours
Repeat CTP in 6 hours before deciding
Perfusion imaging is irrelevant once haemorrhage is excluded
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.answer: The large core predicts poor benefit and higher haemorrhagic transformation risk, arguing against reperfusion
investigations__CT__Head / Brain.explanation: A large established core with minimal penumbra means little salvageable tissue. Reperfusing an already-infarcted volume gives little clinical gain while raising the risk of haemorrhagic transformation. The late-window thrombectomy trials selected patients with SMALL cores and large mismatch; this patient's imaging predicts a poor outcome from intervention.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 34-year-old man with a 5-day history of severe left-sided facial pain, fever and worsening frontal headache develops swelling and redness of the left upper eyelid. On examination he has proptosis, painful restriction of left eye movements and reduced visual acuity. Which is the single most appropriate next imaging investigation?
options: Non-contrast coronal CT of the paranasal sinuses
Contrast-enhanced CT of the sinuses and orbits
MRI of the internal auditory meatus
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Contrast-enhanced CT of the sinuses and orbits
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: Proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia and reduced acuity indicate orbital spread of sinusitis (orbital cellulitis/subperiosteal abscess), an emergency. Contrast-enhanced CT of the sinuses and orbits characterises any abscess and assesses intracranial extension, guiding urgent IV antibiotics and ENT/ophthalmology management. A plain non-contrast sinus CT would miss the enhancing collection; plain films and orbital ultrasound are inadequate; IAM MRI is irrelevant.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: Before functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS), a coronal CT is reviewed for danger variants. Which variant is a posterior ethmoid air cell that lies immediately adjacent to the optic nerve and increases the risk of visual loss during surgery?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: An Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell is a posterior ethmoid cell that extends near the optic nerve and can leave the nerve exposed, risking injury during posterior ethmoidectomy. A Haller cell is an infraorbital ethmoid cell narrowing the OMC; agger nasi is the most anterior ethmoid cell; concha bullosa is a pneumatised middle turbinate; a dehiscent lamina papyracea threatens the orbit rather than the optic nerve directly.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with unilateral facial pain, black nasal crusting and reduced vision. CT sinuses shows unilateral opacification of the ethmoid and maxillary sinuses with bony destruction of the medial orbital wall. Which diagnosis must be excluded most urgently?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: Unilateral sinus opacification with bony destruction in a diabetic/immunocompromised patient, with black necrotic mucosa, is invasive fungal sinusitis (mucormycosis) until proven otherwise. It is rapidly progressive and life-threatening, needing urgent MRI/contrast imaging, biopsy, systemic antifungals and surgical debridement. The other options do not cause aggressive unilateral bone destruction.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 9-year-old boy is hit in the eye by a football. There is little external bruising, but he cannot look upward with the right eye and reports double vision on upgaze. During examination he becomes pale, nauseated and bradycardic. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and review in the fracture clinic in one week
Urgent CT orbits and immediate referral for surgical release
Arrange an MRI orbits to characterise the soft tissues
Patch the eye and give simple analgesia only
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Urgent CT orbits and immediate referral for surgical release
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: This is a paediatric 'white-eyed' trapdoor blowout: minimal external signs, inferior rectus entrapment causing restricted upgaze/vertical diplopia, and the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea). It is a surgical emergency — CT confirms entrapment and the child needs prompt release, not a week's delay.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 6-year-old presents with a swollen, red left eye. She has marked proptosis, pain and restriction on eye movements, and reduced colour vision. She has had a preceding upper respiratory illness. Which finding on CT orbits would most strongly confirm the sight-threatening diagnosis?
options: Enlarged inferior rectus belly sparing the tendon insertion
Teardrop-shaped opacity in the maxillary sinus
Subperiosteal abscess along the lamina papyracea with adjacent ethmoid opacification
Radio-opaque foreign body within the globe
Bilateral symmetrical expansion of the extraocular muscles
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Subperiosteal abscess along the lamina papyracea with adjacent ethmoid opacification
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: Proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia and reduced colour vision indicate post-septal (orbital) cellulitis, typically from ethmoid sinusitis spreading across the lamina papyracea. A subperiosteal abscess there is the key CT finding. The teardrop and tendon-sparing muscle enlargement point to blowout fracture and thyroid eye disease respectively.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 34-year-old welder felt something strike his eye while grinding metal without goggles. Acuity is mildly reduced and there is a small corneal laceration. Which statement about imaging is correct?
options: MRI orbits is the first-line investigation to locate the fragment
CT orbits is appropriate and MRI should be avoided until a metallic foreign body is excluded
Ultrasound of the globe is contraindicated in all penetrating injuries so proceed to MRI
No imaging is required as the fragment is likely radiolucent
Plain radiographs are useless for metallic foreign bodies
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: CT orbits is appropriate and MRI should be avoided until a metallic foreign body is excluded
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A high-velocity metallic fragment from grinding is a classic scenario for a metallic intra-orbital foreign body. CT is excellent for radio-opaque metal/glass. MRI is contraindicated while a ferromagnetic FB is possible because the fragment can move and damage ocular structures; plain films can also detect metal.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 34-year-old man has a 2-year history of foul-smelling discharge from the right ear and progressive hearing loss. Otoscopy shows an attic retraction pocket with crust. HRCT of the temporal bones shows a non-dependent soft-tissue mass in Prussak's space with blunting of the scutum and erosion of the ossicular heads. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic serous otitis media with effusion
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: Foul otorrhoea, an attic retraction pocket, and a NON-dependent soft-tissue mass eroding the scutum and ossicles are the classic clinical and CT features of an acquired (pars flaccida) cholesteatoma. An effusion would be dependent and non-erosive; otosclerosis shows otic capsule lucency without a soft-tissue mass; glomus is a vascular retrotympanic mass.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 6-year-old with acute otitis media develops post-auricular swelling, erythema and a protruding pinna. HRCT shows opacified right mastoid air cells with loss of the intervening bony septa and a small subperiosteal fluid collection. Which single CT finding best confirms the surgical diagnosis of coalescent mastoiditis rather than simple otomastoiditis?
options: Fluid opacification of the mastoid air cells
Loss of the bony septa between mastoid air cells
An air-fluid level in the middle ear
Enlargement of the internal auditory canal
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Loss of the bony septa between mastoid air cells
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: Opacification of the air cells is common in any middle ear/mastoid inflammation and does not by itself indicate surgical disease. Breakdown (coalescence) of the bony septa — here with a subperiosteal abscess — defines coalescent mastoiditis and drives the need for intervention.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 25-year-old is assaulted and sustains a head injury. He has clear fluid dripping from the right ear and audiometry shows a conductive hearing loss on that side. HRCT shows a fracture running along the long axis of the petrous temporal bone with ossicular chain disruption. Which fracture type and the highest-associated risk are correct?
options: Transverse fracture — high risk of immediate facial nerve palsy
Longitudinal fracture — CSF otorrhoea and conductive hearing loss
Transverse fracture — sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Longitudinal fracture — CSF otorrhoea and conductive hearing loss
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A fracture along the long axis is longitudinal (the commoner pattern). It typically spares the otic capsule but disrupts the ossicular chain, producing conductive hearing loss, and is associated with CSF otorrhoea. Transverse fractures cross the axis through the otic capsule and cause sensorineural loss, vertigo and a higher rate of immediate facial nerve injury.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 24-year-old man is assaulted and sustains midface trauma. CT facial bones shows fractures passing horizontally across the maxilla just above the tooth apices, through both pterygoid plates, giving a mobile hard palate on examination. Which fracture pattern does this describe?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A horizontal fracture across the maxilla above the teeth producing a mobile ('floating') palate is a Le Fort I. Le Fort II is pyramidal through the infraorbital rims (floating maxilla) and Le Fort III is craniofacial disjunction (floating face); all Le Fort patterns cross the pterygoid plates. A ZMC fracture involves the cheekbone attachments, and a blowout involves the orbital floor.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 30-year-old woman is struck on the left cheek. She has flattening of the left malar eminence, numbness of the left cheek and upper lip, and limited mouth opening. CT confirms fractures of the zygomaticofrontal suture, zygomatic arch and anterior maxillary wall. Which nerve injury explains her sensory disturbance?
options: Buccal branch of the facial nerve
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A ZMC ('tripod') fracture disrupts the infraorbital rim/floor, injuring the infraorbital nerve (V2), which supplies sensation to the cheek, lower eyelid, side of nose and upper lip. The mental nerve supplies the lower lip/chin, the supraorbital nerve the forehead, the lingual nerve the tongue, and the facial nerve is motor.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 45-year-old man with severe bilateral mandibular (parasymphyseal) fractures after a road traffic collision is becoming increasingly agitated with noisy breathing and reduced oxygen saturations while lying supine. What is the most appropriate immediate priority?
options: Secure the airway while maintaining C-spine immobilisation
Arrange urgent 3D CT reconstruction of the facial skeleton
Refer to maxillofacial surgery for open reduction and internal fixation
Insert an anterior nasal pack to control bleeding
Give intravenous tranexamic acid and reassess
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Secure the airway while maintaining C-spine immobilisation
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A bilateral parasymphyseal 'flail' mandible allows the tongue to fall back and obstruct the airway, worsened when supine. ABC takes priority, so the airway must be secured with C-spine control before imaging or definitive fracture management. Nasal packing is contraindicated/unhelpful here and risks intracranial passage if there is a base-of-skull injury; TXA and surgical referral do not address the immediate airway threat.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 24-year-old presents with a 3-day history of severe sore throat, trismus, a muffled "hot potato" voice and fever. Contrast-enhanced CT neck shows a rim-enhancing low-density collection medial to the left tonsil with deviation of the uvula to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A rim-enhancing collection medial to the tonsil with trismus, a "hot potato" voice and uvular deviation is the classic picture of a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). Retropharyngeal collections sit prevertebrally, Ludwig's is a bilateral submandibular/sublingual cellulitis, and reactive nodes do not form a rim-enhancing tonsillar cavity.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history has a persistent firm right neck lump. Contrast-enhanced CT neck shows a 3 cm right level II node that is rounded with a low-density centre and loss of the fatty hilum. What is the single most appropriate next step?
options: Start a course of oral antibiotics
Urgent 2-week-wait ENT referral for triple assessment
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Urgent 2-week-wait ENT referral for triple assessment
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A persistent neck lump in an older smoker with CT features of a malignant node (rounded, central necrosis, loss of fatty hilum) is head & neck cancer until proven otherwise. It warrants an urgent 2-week-wait ENT referral and triple assessment (examination, imaging, tissue). Antibiotics, delayed review or brain MRI would inappropriately delay diagnosis.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 45-year-old with poor dentition has rapidly progressive bilateral submandibular swelling, drooling, a raised tongue and early stridor. CT neck confirms bilateral sublingual and submandibular cellulitis with tongue elevation. What is the most important immediate priority?
options: Secure the airway with senior anaesthetics/ENT involvement
Give oral analgesia and discharge with review
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Secure the airway with senior anaesthetics/ENT involvement
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: This is Ludwig's angina with impending airway obstruction (drooling, tongue elevation, stridor). Airway management by senior anaesthetics/ENT takes absolute priority, alongside IV antibiotics and surgical drainage. FNA, outpatient dentistry, discharge or further imaging would dangerously delay definitive airway control.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 71-year-old man has a 20-minute episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that fully resolves. CT head is normal. Carotid Doppler then CT angiography show a 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery (NASCET). He is started on aspirin and a high-intensity statin. What is the most appropriate next step in preventing a future stroke?
options: Refer for left carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks
Arrange carotid endarterectomy of the right internal carotid artery
Continue antiplatelet and statin alone with no surgical referral
Start warfarin and repeat imaging in 3 months
Refer for carotid endarterectomy only if a further TIA occurs
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Refer for left carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: This is a symptomatic significant (50–99% NASCET) stenosis on the side appropriate to his right-sided symptoms (left carotid supplies the left hemisphere controlling the right side). NICE recommends carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks of symptom onset plus best medical therapy. The right carotid is asymptomatic here, medical therapy alone is insufficient for a symptomatic tight stenosis, and warfarin is not the treatment for atherosclerotic carotid disease.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with left-sided neck pain, a droopy left eyelid, and transient right-hand clumsiness three days after a whiplash injury. Examination shows left ptosis and miosis. Which CT angiogram finding best fits the likely diagnosis?
options: Tapered 'string sign' narrowing with an intimal flap in the left internal carotid
Calcified plaque at the left carotid bifurcation with 90% stenosis
Complete occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery
Aneurysmal dilatation of the aortic arch
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.answer: Tapered 'string sign' narrowing with an intimal flap in the left internal carotid
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A young patient with neck pain, painful partial Horner's (ptosis + miosis) and focal ischaemia following neck trauma is the classic picture of carotid dissection. CTA shows a tapered flame/string-sign lumen, an intimal flap, or a false lumen from intramural haematoma. Calcified bifurcation plaque describes atherosclerotic stenosis in older patients, not this presentation.

investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.question: A 68-year-old man has had a left hemispheric TIA. CT angiography shows complete (100%) occlusion of the left internal carotid artery. What is the most appropriate management of the occluded vessel?
options: Carotid artery stenting of the occluded segment
Therapeutic anticoagulation with a DOAC as first-line
Bypass grafting of the internal carotid artery
investigations__CT__Neck & Facial.explanation: A fully (100%) occluded internal carotid artery is not revascularised — endarterectomy and stenting are reserved for symptomatic 50–99% stenosis where a residual lumen remains. Management is best medical therapy (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP control, smoking cessation). Anticoagulation is not first-line for atherosclerotic carotid disease.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 72-year-old man attends after a fall from standing height, striking his head. He has neck pain but no neurology. His GCS is 15. Which is the single most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
options: Plain AP and lateral cervical spine radiographs
Flexion-extension radiographs of the cervical spine
No imaging; clear the C-spine clinically
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: Age ≥65 is a Canadian C-spine rule high-risk factor mandating imaging, and CT is preferred over plain films in older/higher-risk patients as it is far more sensitive. Flexion-extension views are unsafe before clearance, MRI is reserved for cord/ligament assessment, and clinical clearance is not permitted with a high-risk factor present.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 25-year-old dives into a shallow pool and strikes the top of his head. CT cervical spine shows fractures of both the anterior and posterior arches of C1 with lateral displacement of the lateral masses. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: A Jefferson fracture is a C1 burst injury caused by axial loading (e.g. diving), producing fractures of the ring of C1 with spread of the lateral masses. Hangman's is a C2 hyperextension injury, the odontoid peg is the C2 dens, and clay-shoveler's affects the C7 spinous process.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: An 80-year-old woman falls forwards and hyperextends her neck. She develops weakness that is worse in the upper limbs than the lower limbs. CT cervical spine shows degenerative change but no fracture. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat CT cervical spine with contrast
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: The picture is central cord syndrome — a hyperextension injury in an elderly patient with disproportionate upper-limb weakness and often no fracture on CT. MRI is required to assess the cord (oedema/signal change), ligaments and discs. CT cannot demonstrate cord injury, and flexion-extension views are unsafe here.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a fall from height, landing on his feet. Trauma CT shows an L1 fracture with loss of vertebral body height, involvement of the posterior vertebral wall, and a bone fragment displaced into the spinal canal. Which single feature best indicates that this injury is unstable?
options: Loss of anterior vertebral body height
Focal kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction
Middle column involvement with retropulsion of bone into the canal
A fracture of the spinous process
investigations__CT__Spine.answer: Middle column involvement with retropulsion of bone into the canal
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: This is a burst fracture. In the Denis 3-column model, middle-column failure (posterior vertebral wall) with retropulsion is the hallmark of instability and cord risk, distinguishing it from a stable anterior-only wedge fracture.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 32-year-old restrained front-seat passenger is admitted after a high-speed collision. CT of the thoracolumbar spine shows a horizontal fracture extending through the anterior, middle and posterior columns of L2. Beyond spinal management, which is the most important immediate additional assessment?
options: Careful evaluation for intra-abdominal (bowel and mesenteric) injury
Nerve conduction studies of the lower limbs
investigations__CT__Spine.answer: Careful evaluation for intra-abdominal (bowel and mesenteric) injury
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: This is a Chance (seat-belt / flexion-distraction) fracture through all three columns. It is classically associated with intra-abdominal injuries — bowel perforation, mesenteric tears and pancreatic injury — which must be actively sought.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 71-year-old woman with no history of trauma presents with progressive thoracic back pain and new leg weakness. CT shows collapse of a mid-thoracic vertebra with bony destruction, posterior wall involvement and a soft-tissue component. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Plain radiograph of the thoracic spine
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: Bony destruction and a soft-tissue mass suggest pathological (malignant) collapse. With new neurology, MRI whole spine is required urgently to assess marrow, detect further metastases and exclude spinal cord compression.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 34-year-old man presents with 2 days of worsening low back pain, numbness around his perineum and difficulty passing urine. On examination he has bilateral leg weakness, reduced anal tone and decreased sensation over the buttocks and inner thighs. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
options: Bladder ultrasound and post-void residual only
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: This is cauda equina syndrome (saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, reduced anal tone, bilateral signs) — a surgical emergency. MRI is the investigation of choice because it directly visualises the compressed cauda equina and any causative disc/tumour/abscess; CT poorly shows neural elements. Urgent MRI and immediate spinal referral for decompression are required.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 20-year-old cricket fast bowler has chronic activity-related low back pain. Imaging shows a defect through the pars interarticularis of L5 with the 'Scottie dog collar' sign, and L5 has slipped forward on S1. Which single term best describes the forward slip?
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: Spondylolysis is the pars interarticularis defect (Scottie dog collar sign). When bilateral defects allow one vertebra to slip forward on the one below (classically L5 on S1), this is spondylolisthesis. Spondylosis refers to general degenerative change, and spinal stenosis is canal narrowing.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 78-year-old woman reports bilateral leg pain and heaviness after walking 100 metres, relieved by sitting or leaning forward on her shopping trolley. Foot pulses are normal. CT lumbar spine shows facet joint hypertrophy and osteophytes narrowing the central canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar canal stenosis
Lumbar disc prolapse with S1 radiculopathy
investigations__CT__Spine.answer: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar canal stenosis
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: Bilateral leg symptoms on walking, relieved by flexion/sitting, with normal pulses and CT showing facet arthropathy/osteophytes narrowing the canal, is classic neurogenic claudication from degenerative lumbar canal stenosis. Preserved pulses argue against vascular claudication, and there are no cauda equina red flags (no saddle anaesthesia or sphincter disturbance).

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 24-year-old is brought in after a high-speed motorcycle crash. Trauma CT shows an L1 burst fracture. He is haemodynamically stable with no other obvious injury. What is the most appropriate next imaging step regarding his spine?
options: No further spinal imaging as the fracture is already identified
Plain radiographs of the cervical spine only
CT of the whole spine to exclude a second non-contiguous fracture
Repeat CT of the lumbar spine in 48 hours
MRI whole spine as first-line to characterise the L1 fracture
investigations__CT__Spine.answer: CT of the whole spine to exclude a second non-contiguous fracture
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: A single spinal fracture mandates whole-spine imaging because ~10–15% of patients have a second, non-contiguous fracture elsewhere in the column. CT is the appropriate modality for bony injury; MRI is added later if there is neurology or suspected cord/ligamentous injury.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A 78-year-old man with known ankylosing spondylitis presents after a simple fall from standing, complaining of neck pain. Which statement best guides your management?
options: A rigid ankylosed spine is protected against fracture, so imaging is rarely needed
Even trivial trauma can cause a highly unstable transverse fracture, so have a very low threshold to CT the whole spine
Plain cervical radiographs reliably exclude fracture in a bamboo spine
Fractures in ankylosing spondylitis are stable and can be managed without immobilisation
MRI is contraindicated so no cross-sectional imaging should be performed
investigations__CT__Spine.answer: Even trivial trauma can cause a highly unstable transverse fracture, so have a very low threshold to CT the whole spine
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: The fused, rigid spine in ankylosing spondylitis/DISH behaves like a long bone and fractures across all three columns even after minor trauma. These transverse fractures are unstable and easily missed on plain films, so whole-spine CT with full spinal precautions is essential.

investigations__CT__Spine.question: A young man with a mid-cervical spinal cord injury is hypotensive (BP 84/50) with a heart rate of 48. He has warm peripheries and no external haemorrhage. What is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
investigations__CT__Spine.explanation: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries after a high cord injury indicates neurogenic shock from disruption of sympathetic outflow. This contrasts with haemorrhagic shock (hypotension with tachycardia). Bleeding must still be actively excluded as the two can coexist.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 34-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of progressive facial swelling, headache worse on bending forward, and distended veins over his upper chest wall. A contrast CT chest shows a bulky lobulated anterior mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava, with associated paratracheal lymphadenopathy. Which is the single most appropriate immediate priority?
options: Reassure and arrange outpatient review in 6 weeks
Recognise superior vena cava obstruction as an oncological emergency and arrange urgent oncology/MDT input and tissue diagnosis
Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed mediastinitis
Request an HRCT to characterise the lung parenchyma
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.answer: Recognise superior vena cava obstruction as an oncological emergency and arrange urgent oncology/MDT input and tissue diagnosis
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Facial/upper-limb swelling, plethora and distended chest-wall veins with an anterior mediastinal mass (here likely lymphoma) is SVC obstruction — an oncological emergency. It needs urgent imaging (already done), urgent oncology/MDT referral and tissue diagnosis to guide treatment. Antibiotics and warfarin do not address the cause, and delay is unsafe.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 71-year-old retired shipyard worker has a right pleural effusion and breathlessness. Contrast CT chest shows nodular, circumferential pleural thickening measuring 1.5 cm, involving the mediastinal pleural surface, with volume loss of the hemithorax. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Nodular, circumferential pleural thickening >1 cm with mediastinal pleural involvement are the classic CT features of malignant pleural disease; in a patient with asbestos exposure (shipyard) this strongly suggests mesothelioma. A simple parapneumonic effusion causes smooth, thin pleural change; sarcoid and PE do not produce this pattern; bronchogenic cysts are middle-mediastinal, not pleural.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 58-year-old woman with pneumonia remains febrile despite antibiotics. Contrast CT chest shows a loculated pleural collection with enhancement and thickening of both the visceral and parietal pleura, separated by fluid. Which sign is described and what does it indicate?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Enhancement and thickening of the visceral and parietal pleura separated by a loculated collection is the split pleura sign, characteristic of an empyema — which typically requires drainage in addition to antibiotics. The other signs describe unrelated parenchymal/airway findings.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 68-year-old smoker has an 18 mm right upper lobe nodule found incidentally. Non-contrast CT shows an irregular, spiculated margin with no calcification. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge, no further imaging
Refer to the respiratory MDT for PET-CT/biopsy work-up
Start empirical antibiotics and repeat CXR in 6 weeks
Attribute the appearance to old tuberculosis
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.answer: Refer to the respiratory MDT for PET-CT/biopsy work-up
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Spiculation, size, upper-lobe location and a smoking history in an older patient are all malignant features. Under UK/BTS guidance this warrants prompt work-up with PET-CT and/or biopsy via the respiratory MDT, with a 2-week-wait referral if lung cancer is suspected — not dismissal or a 5-year interval.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 55-year-old woman has a 9 mm nodule on CT with a well-defined smooth margin, popcorn calcification and internal fat attenuation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Popcorn calcification together with intralesional fat is characteristic of a benign pulmonary hamartoma. Fat and benign calcification patterns are reassuring features that essentially exclude malignancy, so no aggressive work-up is needed.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 40-year-old man with an eGFR of 22 mL/min needs CT of the chest to characterise a lung nodule seen on chest X-ray. Which is the most appropriate imaging choice?
options: CT chest with high-volume iodinated contrast
No imaging — repeat chest X-ray in 2 years
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: IV iodinated contrast is relatively contraindicated with significant renal impairment (contrast-associated nephropathy risk). A nodule can be characterised on non-contrast CT for size, margins, calcification and fat, so a low-dose non-contrast protocol is the appropriate choice, applying ALARA.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: On a non-contrast CT chest, which finding is a benign marker of previous asbestos exposure rather than active malignancy?
options: Eccentric calcification within a growing mass
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Calcified pleural plaques are benign and act as a marker of asbestos exposure. They are not malignant themselves, though they should prompt review for symptoms of asbestos-related disease such as mesothelioma.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 68-year-old ex-smoker presents with 12 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. Examination reveals fine bibasal inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern with reduced TLCO. HRCT shows peripheral, subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, without significant ground-glass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: A UIP pattern on HRCT (subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) in an older patient with clubbing, bibasal crackles and a restrictive defect with reduced TLCO is characteristic of IPF. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis and sarcoidosis typically favour the upper/mid zones; PCP causes ground-glass, not honeycombing; chronic PE would not produce this parenchymal pattern.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 34-year-old man with HIV (not on antiretrovirals, CD4 count 90) presents with 2 weeks of dry cough, fever and progressive breathlessness with marked exertional desaturation. HRCT shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacification with a perihilar predominance and no honeycombing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacification with exertional desaturation in a profoundly immunocompromised patient (CD4 <200) is classic for PCP. Ground-glass reflects an active alveolar/inflammatory process rather than established fibrosis. The absence of honeycombing and the acute course argue against IPF, asbestosis and silicosis; bronchiectasis produces airway dilatation, not diffuse ground-glass.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 45-year-old woman is investigated for chronic productive cough with recurrent chest infections and occasional haemoptysis. HRCT shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi that fail to taper, with several bronchi appearing wider than their accompanying pulmonary artery. Which HRCT sign best describes this finding?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: A bronchus dilated wider than its adjacent pulmonary artery forms the signet-ring sign, the hallmark of bronchiectasis, alongside lack of tapering and wall thickening. Honeycombing indicates end-stage fibrosis; the halo sign describes ground-glass around a nodule (e.g. invasive aspergillosis); tree-in-bud reflects small-airway/endobronchial infection; mosaic attenuation reflects small-airways disease or vascular causes.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 58-year-old man presents with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness 6 days after a total knee replacement. He is tachycardic and hypoxic. His two-level Wells score for PE is 6. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: A Wells score >4 means PE is 'likely', so NICE directs immediate CTPA — the first-line definitive test — without a preceding D-dimer. D-dimer belongs only in the 'PE unlikely' (Wells ≤4) arm. Interim anticoagulation is given if CTPA is delayed.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 34-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant presents with breathlessness and a raised clinical suspicion of PE. She has normal renal function and no contrast allergy. Which imaging option is most appropriate to consider as an alternative to CTPA?
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: In pregnancy (and where CTPA is contraindicated by renal impairment or contrast allergy), a V/Q scan is the recommended alternative for imaging suspected PE. D-dimer is unhelpful in pregnancy because it is physiologically raised and non-specific.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 61-year-old woman with a confirmed PE on CTPA becomes hypotensive (BP 78/45) and drowsy. The CTPA report notes RV dilatation with an RV:LV ratio greater than 1. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: IV fluids and repeat CTPA in 24 hours
Insert an inferior vena cava filter
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: This is a massive (high-risk) PE with haemodynamic instability and right heart strain (RV:LV >1). It is a peri-arrest emergency requiring thrombolysis (e.g. alteplase), or embolectomy if thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated. A DOAC alone is inadequate for an unstable, massive PE.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 68-year-old smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss has a right hilar mass on CXR. A contrast-enhanced staging CT chest is arranged. To which anatomical extent should the scan be taken to complete initial staging?
options: Chest only, from lung apices to costophrenic angles
Chest plus upper abdomen to include the liver and adrenals
Chest plus a dedicated CT head in the same acquisition
Chest plus whole pelvis to assess for bony metastases
Chest plus lower limbs to exclude DVT before surgery
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.answer: Chest plus upper abdomen to include the liver and adrenals
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: The first-line staging CT for lung cancer covers the chest and extends through the upper abdomen to include the liver and adrenals, which are common metastatic sites. The brain is not routinely covered by this scan and needs dedicated contrast CT or MRI head when indicated; pelvis/lower limbs are not part of standard staging.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A patient with biopsy-proven non-small-cell lung cancer has a peripheral primary on CT with borderline enlarged subcarinal nodes. The MDT needs to confirm whether the mediastinal nodes are involved before deciding on surgery. Which investigation best confirms the nodal (N) stage?
options: Repeat contrast-enhanced CT chest in 3 months
PET-CT alone as definitive nodal proof
CT-guided biopsy of the peripheral primary
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: EBUS-TBNA samples mediastinal nodes to obtain tissue and confirm the N stage, which is decisive for resectability. PET-CT characterises nodes functionally and guides where to sample but is not definitive tissue proof. CT-guided biopsy of the peripheral primary confirms the primary histology, not nodal status, and brain MRI addresses M staging.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 60-year-old presents with right arm pain, wasting of the small muscles of the hand, and a right-sided ptosis and miosis. CXR shows a right apical opacity. Which single statement best fits this presentation?
options: This is a Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumour causing Horner's syndrome, requiring urgent assessment and staging
This is most likely small-cell carcinoma that is always operable at this stage
This is SVC obstruction and mandates immediate thrombolysis
Horner's syndrome here excludes malignancy and suggests a benign cause
No 2-week-wait referral is needed as symptoms are musculoskeletal
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.answer: This is a Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumour causing Horner's syndrome, requiring urgent assessment and staging
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: An apical (superior sulcus/Pancoast) tumour invading the sympathetic chain and brachial plexus produces Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), arm pain and T1 wasting — a red-flag presentation needing urgent 2-week-wait referral and staging CT. It is not SVC obstruction, is not benign, and there is no basis to call it operable small-cell disease.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 62-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history (stopped 4 years ago) attends a lung health check. He is asymptomatic. A validated risk model classifies him as high-risk. According to the NHS lung cancer screening programme, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Chest X-ray as the primary screening test
Reassure and discharge as he has stopped smoking
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: He is an asymptomatic high-risk ever-smoker in the eligible age range, so the correct screening test is low-dose non-contrast CT chest (as in NLST/NELSON and the UK Targeted Lung Health Check programme). Chest X-ray is not the screening modality (it did not reduce mortality in trials). PET-CT and biopsy are for nodule work-up, not first-line screening. Having stopped smoking recently does not remove his elevated risk.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: Which of the following is the best example of a harm of LDCT lung cancer screening rather than a benefit?
options: Identification of high-risk individuals for surveillance
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: Overdiagnosis — detecting indolent cancers that would never have caused harm, leading to unnecessary treatment — is a recognised harm of screening, alongside false positives, radiation and incidental findings. Earlier-stage operable cancer, reduced mortality, cessation support and risk-based selection are benefits or strengths of the programme.

investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.question: A 58-year-old woman enrolled in a lung screening programme develops a 4-week history of haemoptysis and 5 kg unintentional weight loss before her next scheduled LDCT. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wait for her next scheduled routine screening LDCT
Refer via the urgent 2-week-wait symptomatic cancer pathway
Reassure as she is already in the screening programme
Repeat the risk assessment model and rescreen in 12 months
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.answer: Refer via the urgent 2-week-wait symptomatic cancer pathway
investigations__CT__Chest / Lung.explanation: She now has red-flag symptoms of possible lung cancer (haemoptysis, weight loss). Screening is for asymptomatic people; symptomatic patients must be referred on the urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway for prompt investigation, not left to routine screening intervals.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 58-year-old man reports a 3-month history of central chest tightness that comes on when walking uphill and settles within a few minutes of resting. He has no chest pain at rest. His resting ECG is normal. According to current NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate first-line investigation?
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: This is stable exertional chest pain with features of typical/atypical angina. Updated NICE guidance makes CTCA the first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected coronary origin. Exercise ECG is no longer recommended as the first-line anatomical test, invasive angiography is reserved for cases where non-invasive testing is inconclusive or high-risk, functional imaging follows CTCA if obstructive disease is uncertain, and troponin is for suspected ACS, not stable chest pain.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 62-year-old woman with atypical exertional chest pain undergoes CTCA, which is reported as showing no coronary plaque and normal coronary arteries. Which statement best reflects the clinical value of this result?
options: It confirms she has significant obstructive coronary artery disease
It effectively excludes significant obstructive coronary artery disease
It cannot comment on non-calcified plaque
It mandates invasive coronary angiography for confirmation
It has poor negative predictive value so must be repeated
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.answer: It effectively excludes significant obstructive coronary artery disease
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: CTCA has a very high negative predictive value, so a normal scan effectively rules out significant obstructive CAD and further cardiac testing is generally unnecessary. CTCA visualises both calcified and non-calcified plaque, so it does comment on soft plaque, and a normal result does not require confirmation by invasive angiography.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 40 minutes of severe crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm, associated with sweating and nausea, that started at rest. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation pathway?
options: 12-lead ECG and troponin, following the ACS pathway
Reassure and arrange elective CTCA in clinic
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.answer: 12-lead ECG and troponin, following the ACS pathway
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: This is an acute presentation suggestive of acute coronary syndrome, not stable chest pain. The correct pathway is immediate 12-lead ECG and troponin, with primary PCI for a STEMI. CTCA is a first-line test for STABLE chest pain and is not the primary investigation in suspected ACS; an elective/outpatient approach or calcium score would be unsafe in this acute setting.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 54-year-old asymptomatic man with a family history of early coronary disease has an uncertain calculated cardiovascular risk. His GP arranges a coronary artery calcium score, which returns an Agatston score of 0. What does this most appropriately indicate?
options: He has obstructive coronary artery disease requiring angiography
He is at very low risk of a coronary event over the coming years
He definitely has no soft (non-calcified) plaque
He should start dual antiplatelet therapy immediately
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.answer: He is at very low risk of a coronary event over the coming years
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: An Agatston score of 0 means no identifiable calcified plaque and carries a strong negative predictive value, indicating a very low risk of coronary events. It does not exclude soft plaque, and no acute or antiplatelet treatment is indicated in an asymptomatic patient.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 62-year-old woman is investigated for stable exertional chest pain. Her coronary artery calcium score is ≥400 (extensive calcification). Which statement best reflects the interpretation of this result?
options: A high calcium score confirms a flow-limiting coronary stenosis
The score alone diagnoses acute coronary syndrome
She has a high atherosclerotic burden but obstruction should be assessed with CTCA or functional testing
Statin therapy should be stopped as the disease is fixed
The finding excludes the need for any further cardiac assessment
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.answer: She has a high atherosclerotic burden but obstruction should be assessed with CTCA or functional testing
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: A score ≥400 signifies extensive calcification and high risk, but calcium burden does not prove obstructive stenosis. Assessment of flow limitation requires CTCA (contrast, showing the lumen and soft plaque) or functional testing, alongside aggressive risk-factor and statin management.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute, ongoing central chest pain and sweating. Which is the most appropriate immediate approach?
options: Arrange a non-contrast coronary calcium score to guide management
Follow the ACS pathway with ECG and serial troponin
Reassure and discharge if a previous calcium score was 0
Perform calcium scoring before any blood tests
Start a statin and review in clinic in six weeks
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.answer: Follow the ACS pathway with ECG and serial troponin
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: A calcium score is a risk/burden marker, not a test for acute chest pain. Acute cardiac chest pain must be managed via the ACS pathway with ECG and troponin. A previous score of 0 does not exclude acute coronary syndrome and must not delay assessment.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 62-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. His BP is 178/96 in the right arm and 132/74 in the left arm, and CXR shows a widened mediastinum. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT angiography of the aorta (CT aortogram)
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.answer: CT angiography of the aorta (CT aortogram)
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: Tearing pain, an inter-arm BP differential and a wide mediastinum strongly suggest aortic dissection. In a stable patient, CT aortogram is the definitive test — it demonstrates the intimal flap and false lumen and defines Stanford type to guide management. Echo may help but is not definitive for the whole aorta; D-dimer cannot exclude it reliably; coronary angiography and V/Q address other diagnoses.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A CT aortogram in a 58-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome shows an intimal flap involving the ascending aorta and extending into the arch. She is in severe pain with a new early diastolic murmur. What is the most appropriate management?
options: IV labetalol and medical management alone
Oral bisoprolol and repeat CT in 6 weeks
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: Ascending aortic involvement makes this a Stanford Type A dissection, which is a surgical emergency (risk of tamponade, aortic regurgitation — hence the diastolic murmur — and malperfusion). It requires urgent cardiothoracic surgery. BP control is supportive but is not sufficient alone; thrombolysis would be dangerous.

investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.question: A 74-year-old man collapses with sudden severe abdominal and back pain. He has a pulsatile abdominal mass, is pale and sweaty, with BP 78/44 and HR 122. He has a known 6 cm AAA. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Urgent CT aortogram before any intervention
Immediate transfer to theatre for surgery
Abdominal ultrasound in the emergency department
IV labetalol to lower blood pressure
CT of the head to exclude other causes
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.answer: Immediate transfer to theatre for surgery
investigations__CT__Cardiac & Aorta.explanation: This is a ruptured AAA in a haemodynamically unstable patient — pain, pulsatile mass and hypotension. He must go straight to theatre; imaging must not delay definitive surgery. CT aortogram is reserved for the stable patient to plan EVAR vs open repair. Aggressive BP lowering could worsen perfusion, and permissive hypotension is preferred pre-operatively.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with 24 hours of migratory right iliac fossa pain, fever and anorexia. A portal venous CT abdomen/pelvis is performed. Which combination of findings would most strongly confirm acute appendicitis?
options: A collapsed appendix measuring 4 mm with no surrounding change
A blind-ending tubular structure measuring 9 mm with wall enhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding and an appendicolith
Sigmoid colonic wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding
Dilated small-bowel loops with a transition point in the right iliac fossa
Free air tracking beneath both hemidiaphragms
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: A blind-ending tubular structure measuring 9 mm with wall enhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding and an appendicolith
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Acute appendicitis is diagnosed on CT by a dilated (>6 mm), non-compressible appendix with wall enhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding and often an appendicolith. A 4 mm collapsed appendix is normal. Sigmoid wall thickening suggests diverticulitis, a small-bowel transition point suggests obstruction, and free air suggests perforation.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 78-year-old man with abdominal distension and absolute constipation has a portal venous CT showing dilated small-bowel loops (up to 4 cm) with a clear transition point, and a segment of bowel wall that fails to enhance with adjacent intramural gas. Which finding most urgently mandates emergency surgical review?
options: Non-enhancement of the bowel wall with pneumatosis intestinalis
A moderate volume of simple free fluid
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: Non-enhancement of the bowel wall with pneumatosis intestinalis
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Bowel-wall non-enhancement plus pneumatosis intestinalis indicates bowel ischaemia/infarction — a surgical emergency requiring urgent resuscitation and operative review. Dilatation, a transition point, simple free fluid and mild fat stranding are expected in obstruction but do not by themselves signify a non-viable bowel.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 65-year-old man presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and generalised peritonism. The reporting radiologist wants to confidently identify or exclude a small pneumoperitoneum on his portal venous CT. Which review strategy is most appropriate?
options: Review only soft-tissue windows in the dependent pelvis
Review lung/bone windows looking under the diaphragm and in the non-dependent anterior abdomen
Rely on arterial-phase images of the mesenteric vessels
Assess only the portal and mesenteric veins for gas
Limit review to the solid organs for laceration
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: Review lung/bone windows looking under the diaphragm and in the non-dependent anterior abdomen
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Small volumes of free air are best detected on lung or bone windows, and free gas collects in the non-dependent anterior abdomen and beneath the diaphragm in a supine patient. Free air means perforation until proven otherwise. The other strategies target different pathologies (vascular, solid-organ) or dependent locations where free air is less conspicuous.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 44-year-old man presents with severe left loin-to-groin pain and visible haematuria. His eGFR is 38 mL/min and he has a documented previous anaphylactoid reaction to iodinated contrast. What is the most appropriate first-line imaging?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: CT KUB is the gold-standard first-line test for ureteric colic and detects nearly all stones as high-density foci. It requires no IV contrast, making it ideal here given both renal impairment and contrast allergy. Contrast-based studies (urogram, gadolinium) are contraindicated/unnecessary, and IVU has been superseded by CT KUB.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A non-contrast CT abdomen/pelvis in a hypotensive trauma patient shows free fluid in the pelvis and paracolic gutters measuring approximately 55 HU. What does this finding most likely represent?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Fresh blood is hyperdense (~45–70 HU), well above simple fluid such as ascites, urine or bile (~0–15 HU). In a hypotensive trauma patient, hyperdense free fluid indicates haemoperitoneum from active bleeding — resuscitate and escalate urgently to surgery or interventional radiology.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 3 cm right adrenal nodule is found incidentally. On the non-contrast series it measures 6 HU. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: An adrenal lesion measuring ≤10 HU on non-contrast CT is characteristic of a lipid-rich (benign) adenoma — the low density reflects intracellular fat. Metastases, phaeochromocytoma and carcinoma are typically denser (>10 HU) and need washout characterisation; acute haemorrhage would be hyperdense.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 62-year-old man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis has a 3 cm liver nodule found on surveillance ultrasound. Triple-phase CT shows the nodule enhancing brightly on the arterial phase and becoming hypodense relative to liver on the portal venous and delayed phases, with a thin enhancing rim. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Arterial hyperenhancement with portal/delayed washout and a capsule in a cirrhotic liver is the essentially diagnostic ('wash-in and washout') signature of HCC — no biopsy required. Haemangioma fills in centripetally, FNH has a central scar, a cyst does not enhance, and an abscess is rim-enhancing with a fluid centre.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 45-year-old asymptomatic woman has an incidental 2 cm liver lesion. On triple-phase CT it shows peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement on the arterial phase, then progressive centripetal fill-in that matches the blood pool on delayed images. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with centripetal (outside-in) fill-in following the blood pool is the classic pattern of a cavernous haemangioma, the commonest benign liver lesion. HCC washes out, FNH has a central scar, and metastases are typically hypodense on portal venous phase.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 58-year-old man being staged for colorectal cancer has a triple-phase liver CT. Which phase is most sensitive for detecting his likely hypovascular liver metastases, and how will they appear?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Colorectal metastases are usually hypovascular. On the portal venous phase the normal liver parenchyma enhances maximally, so hypovascular metastases stand out as hypodense (dark) lesions against the bright liver — making this the most sensitive phase. Hypervascular metastases (neuroendocrine, RCC, melanoma, thyroid) are instead best seen on the arterial phase.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 68-year-old man presents with painless jaundice, weight loss and pale stools. A pancreatic-protocol CT shows a 3 cm hypoenhancing mass in the pancreatic head with dilatation of both the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. There is no vascular contact and no metastases. Which single feature on CT is MOST important in determining whether he can be offered curative surgery?
options: The size of the primary mass
Degree of contact/encasement of the SMA, coeliac axis and SMV/portal vein
The presence of the double duct sign
The density of the mass on the pancreatic phase
Dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: Degree of contact/encasement of the SMA, coeliac axis and SMV/portal vein
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Resectability of pancreatic adenocarcinoma is determined chiefly by vascular involvement (plus absence of metastases). Encasement >180 degrees of the SMA, coeliac axis or SMV/portal vein usually renders the tumour locally advanced/unresectable. Size, the double duct sign and duct dilatation reflect the tumour and obstruction but do not themselves define operability.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 45-year-old woman is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a lipase five times the upper limit of normal. She is diagnosed with acute pancreatitis. On day 1 the team requests a CT abdomen. What is the MOST appropriate advice regarding CT imaging?
options: Urgent CT now is required to confirm the diagnosis
CT is not needed for early diagnosis; reserve contrast-enhanced CT for ~72h+ to assess severity/complications
An immediate CT is needed to exclude pancreatic cancer
MRCP should replace CT as the first-line diagnostic test on admission
CT should be avoided entirely in acute pancreatitis
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: CT is not needed for early diagnosis; reserve contrast-enhanced CT for ~72h+ to assess severity/complications
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Acute pancreatitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by amylase/lipase. Early CT can appear falsely normal because necrosis has not yet declared. Contrast-enhanced CT at around 72h+ assesses severity and complications (necrosis, collections). CT is not avoided altogether, and MRCP is used later for ductal/biliary assessment, not as the admission diagnostic test.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 52-year-old man with severe gallstone pancreatitis remains septic on day 10 despite antibiotics. A contrast-enhanced CT shows a non-enhancing pancreatic body with a surrounding collection that contains locules of gas. Which is the MOST likely diagnosis and appropriate concern?
options: Infected pancreatic necrosis, which is life-threatening and may need drainage/necrosectomy
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: Infected pancreatic necrosis, which is life-threatening and may need drainage/necrosectomy
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Non-enhancing pancreatic parenchyma indicates necrosis, and gas within the collection (in the absence of instrumentation) signifies infected necrosis. This is a life-threatening complication requiring HDU/ITU care, specialist input and often intervention (percutaneous/endoscopic drainage or necrosectomy). A simple pseudocyst does not contain gas, and the acute septic picture argues against malignancy.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 58-year-old smoker presents with a single episode of painless visible haematuria. Urine dip shows blood only; no nitrites or leucocytes. His eGFR is normal. What is the most appropriate imaging investigation to identify an upper-tract cause?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Painless visible haematuria in a smoker aged ≥45 mandates urgent 2-week-wait work-up. CT urogram is the investigation of choice for the upper tract (renal and urothelial tumours) because its excretory phase opacifies the collecting system to reveal filling defects. He also needs flexible cystoscopy for the bladder. CT KUB and ultrasound miss small urothelial tumours; IVU is largely obsolete.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A CT urogram in a 65-year-old with visible haematuria shows, on the delayed excretory phase, an irregular filling defect within the contrast-opacified right renal pelvis. The non-contrast phase shows no calcification at this site. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: A filling defect in the opacified collecting system on the excretory phase, without corresponding density on the non-contrast phase, is a urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma until proven otherwise. A radiolucent stone would still be dense on the non-contrast CT phase, excluding it. RCC and angiomyolipoma are parenchymal masses, not intraluminal filling defects; a simple cyst does not cause a filling defect.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 50-year-old woman is referred with two episodes of visible haematuria attributed by her GP to a urinary tract infection, though cultures were negative. Which statement is most correct regarding her management?
options: Visible haematuria with negative cultures can be safely observed with repeat urinalysis
She should have a CT urogram and flexible cystoscopy on a 2-week-wait pathway
Renal ultrasound alone is sufficient to exclude urological malignancy
Cystoscopy is unnecessary if the CT urogram is normal
A course of empirical antibiotics should be tried before any referral
