investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: She should have a CT urogram and flexible cystoscopy on a 2-week-wait pathway
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: Visible haematuria is urological cancer until proven otherwise and must not be attributed to a UTI without excluding malignancy. NICE mandates urgent 2-week-wait referral; the work-up is CT urogram (upper tract) plus flexible cystoscopy (bladder — the commonest site). Cystoscopy remains essential even if CTU is normal, as most tumours are in the bladder. Ultrasound alone and observation are inadequate.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: Regarding the phases of a CT urogram, which acquisition best demonstrates a small enhancing renal cell carcinoma within the renal parenchyma?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: The nephrographic phase (roughly 90–100 seconds post-injection) gives uniform enhancement of the renal parenchyma, against which an enhancing solid mass such as an RCC stands out most conspicuously. The non-contrast phase shows calculi but not enhancement; the excretory phase opacifies the collecting system to show intraluminal filling defects (urothelial tumours) rather than parenchymal masses.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 34-year-old man presents with sudden severe right-sided colicky loin-to-groin pain and dipstick haematuria. He is restless and cannot get comfortable. Observations are normal and he is afebrile. Which is the most appropriate first-line imaging investigation?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: NICE recommends urgent low-dose non-contrast CT KUB as first-line/gold-standard for suspected renal colic, ideally within 24 hours. It detects nearly all stones including radiolucent uric acid stones. Contrast is not needed and would obscure calcific stones. Ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy/children but is less sensitive; plain films and IVU are outdated for acute colic.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 58-year-old woman with a known 7 mm obstructing distal ureteric stone becomes pyrexial (39.2°C), tachycardic and hypotensive. CT confirms an obstructed kidney with pyonephrosis. What is the most appropriate immediate management in addition to IV antibiotics and resuscitation?
options: Oral tamsulosin and discharge with follow-up
Urgent decompression with percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteric stent
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.answer: Urgent decompression with percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteric stent
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: An obstructed, infected kidney is a urological emergency. Alongside IV antibiotics and resuscitation, the collecting system must be decompressed urgently by nephrostomy or ureteric stent. Definitive stone treatment (ESWL/PCNL/URS) is deferred until sepsis is controlled. Medical expulsive therapy is inappropriate in the septic obstructed patient.

investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.question: A 72-year-old man attends with acute left flank pain radiating to the groin, presumed renal colic. He is hypotensive with a pulsatile abdominal mass. Which diagnosis must be actively excluded before attributing his symptoms to a ureteric stone?
investigations__CT__Abdomen & Pelvis.explanation: A leaking/ruptured AAA classically masquerades as 'renal colic' in older patients and is rapidly fatal if missed. A hypotensive elderly patient with flank pain and a pulsatile mass must be assumed to have a leaking AAA until proven otherwise — this is why first presentations of 'renal colic' in older adults warrant careful assessment and imaging.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) presents with sudden, severe central abdominal pain. His abdomen is soft with mild tenderness only, but he is in agony. Lactate is 5.2 mmol/L with a metabolic acidosis. Which is the single most appropriate investigation?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: Pain out of proportion to examination with AF and a raised lactate is acute mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise. Arterial-phase CT mesenteric angiography is the investigation of choice, demonstrating the SMA occlusion and late signs of bowel ischaemia. Other modalities lack the speed or vascular detail required in this time-critical emergency.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A CT mesenteric angiogram in a patient with acute mesenteric ischaemia shows an abrupt filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery, non-enhancing small-bowel loops, pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas. What do these findings most indicate?
options: Established transmural bowel infarction requiring surgery
Contrast artefact of no clinical significance
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.answer: Established transmural bowel infarction requiring surgery
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: Bowel-wall non-enhancement, pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas are late, ominous signs of established transmural infarction. This mandates resuscitation, revascularisation and resection of necrotic bowel — an emergency laparotomy — not conservative management.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 68-year-old woman has a large, ongoing lower GI bleed and remains tachycardic despite fluids. CT angiography shows a focal contrast blush pooling within the sigmoid colon lumen. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as the bleed has stopped
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: A contrast blush on CT angiography indicates active extravasation and localises the bleeding point. In an unstable patient this guides catheter angiography and transcatheter embolisation of the culprit vessel (or surgery). A positive CT blush requires ongoing brisk bleeding, so the bleed has not stopped.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 79-year-old frail woman with iron-deficiency anaemia and a change in bowel habit is referred on a 2-week-wait pathway. Colonoscopy is attempted but the endoscope cannot pass a tight, tortuous sigmoid and the examination is abandoned. What is the most appropriate next investigation to assess the whole colon?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: After an incomplete colonoscopy, CT colonography is the standard way to assess the remaining/proximal colon, and it is well tolerated in frail patients without sedation. Barium studies and ultrasound are inferior for detecting colorectal cancer and polyps; flexible sigmoidoscopy would not assess the proximal colon.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 68-year-old man undergoes CT colonography for weight loss and rectal bleeding. Imaging shows a short annular constricting "apple-core" lesion in the descending colon with luminal narrowing. What is the single most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat CTC in 12 months
Colonoscopy for biopsy and refer to the colorectal MDT
Prescribe laxatives and review in clinic
Perform a barium enema for confirmation
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.answer: Colonoscopy for biopsy and refer to the colorectal MDT
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: An apple-core lesion is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. CTC cannot obtain tissue, so colonoscopy with biopsy is needed for a histological diagnosis, alongside staging and colorectal MDT referral. Watchful waiting, laxatives or empirical chemotherapy without tissue diagnosis are inappropriate.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: Which statement about CT colonography is correct?
options: It allows polyps to be removed at the same sitting
It requires colonic insufflation, usually with CO₂, to distend the bowel
It does not require any bowel preparation
It is the first-line UK bowel-cancer screening test for all patients
It is the investigation of choice in suspected acute severe colitis
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.answer: It requires colonic insufflation, usually with CO₂, to distend the bowel
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: CTC needs colonic distension by CO₂/gas insufflation plus bowel preparation to visualise the mucosa. It cannot remove polyps (diagnostic only). UK screening uses FIT then colonoscopy, not CTC first-line. Insufflation is relatively contraindicated in acute severe colitis due to perforation risk.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 24-year-old man with terminal-ileal Crohn's disease is having CT enterography to assess disease activity. Why is he asked to drink a large volume of a neutral (low-density) oral contrast agent before the scan?
options: To opacify the lumen brightly so any perforation is obvious
To distend the small bowel so mural thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement can be seen
To reduce the radiation dose required for the study
To replace the need for intravenous contrast
To coat the colonic mucosa for polyp detection
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.answer: To distend the small bowel so mural thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement can be seen
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: A neutral agent keeps the lumen low-density and distends the small bowel, allowing wall thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement to be appreciated. A dense (positive) agent would brighten the lumen and mask wall enhancement. IV contrast is still given in addition.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 30-year-old woman with Crohn's disease undergoes CT enterography. The report describes engorged, comb-like vasa recta running to an inflamed ileal loop alongside surrounding fibrofatty proliferation. Which single term best describes the vascular appearance?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: The comb sign is engorged vasa recta arranged like the teeth of a comb supplying an actively inflamed segment — a marker of active Crohn's. The fibrofatty change is 'creeping fat'. The other signs relate to volvulus/obstruction or other pathology.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 45-year-old man with long-standing Crohn's presents with colicky pain, distension and vomiting. CT enterography shows a short segment of fixed, non-enhancing small-bowel narrowing with marked pre-stenotic dilatation and no significant mural hyperenhancement. What does this most likely represent and imply for management?
options: Active inflammatory stricture — escalate biologic therapy
Fibrotic stricture causing obstruction — likely needs surgical or endoscopic management
Normal collapsed bowel — no action needed
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.answer: Fibrotic stricture causing obstruction — likely needs surgical or endoscopic management
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: A fixed, non-enhancing narrowing with pre-stenotic dilatation and obstructive symptoms indicates a fibrotic (rather than active inflammatory) stricture, which responds poorly to medical therapy and typically requires surgery or endoscopic dilatation with MDT input. An enhancing, oedematous wall would instead suggest active disease treatable medically.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 58-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm right adrenal nodule found incidentally on a staging CT. On a dedicated adrenal protocol, the non-contrast attenuation is 6 HU. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Proceed to CT-guided biopsy of the nodule
No further imaging characterisation is required — this is a lipid-rich adenoma
Calculate the absolute and relative washout
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.answer: No further imaging characterisation is required — this is a lipid-rich adenoma
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: A non-contrast attenuation ≤10 HU (here 6 HU) is diagnostic of a benign lipid-rich adenoma, so no washout calculation or further imaging is needed. (A functional biochemical screen is still indicated, but imaging characterisation is complete.) Washout is only calculated for lipid-poor lesions >10 HU.

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A lipid-poor left adrenal lesion (28 HU non-contrast) is characterised with washout CT: venous phase 78 HU, 15-minute delayed phase 42 HU. Which value and interpretation is correct?
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: Absolute washout = (venous − delayed) / (venous − non-contrast) = (78 − 42) / (78 − 28) = 36/50 = 72%. A value ≥60% indicates rapid de-enhancement typical of a benign adenoma. (Relative washout here = 36/78 = 46%, also ≥40%, consistent.)

investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.question: A 44-year-old man with episodic headaches, palpitations and labile hypertension has a 3 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass with low washout. What is the single most important step before any biopsy or surgical manipulation?
options: Start a beta-blocker to control blood pressure
Measure plasma/urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma
Perform an overnight dexamethasone suppression test
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.answer: Measure plasma/urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma
investigations__CT__GI & Vascular.explanation: The clinical picture and imaging suggest a possible phaeochromocytoma. Biopsy or manipulation of an unblocked phaeo can precipitate a life-threatening hypertensive crisis, so it must be excluded biochemically (metanephrines) first. Note also that starting an unopposed beta-blocker in a phaeo is dangerous — alpha-blockade must precede beta-blockade.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 24-year-old man falls onto an outstretched hand. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Plain wrist radiographs, including scaphoid views, are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with simple analgesia and reassurance
Immobilise the wrist and re-image with CT or MRI
Arrange immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Repeat identical plain radiographs the same day
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: Immobilise the wrist and re-image with CT or MRI
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness with a normal initial X-ray is treated as a clinical scaphoid fracture. The wrist is immobilised and re-imaged with CT or MRI to detect an occult fracture, because a missed scaphoid fracture risks non-union and avascular necrosis. Discharge or ignoring the injury is unsafe, and surgery is not indicated before a fracture is even confirmed.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A proximal pole scaphoid fracture is confirmed on CT. Which feature of scaphoid anatomy explains why this fracture is particularly prone to avascular necrosis?
options: Dual blood supply from radial and ulnar arteries
Antegrade blood supply entering the proximal pole
Blood supply derived solely from the interosseous membrane
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: The scaphoid receives a retrograde blood supply that enters distally, so a proximal pole fracture cuts off perfusion to the proximal fragment, causing a high rate of avascular necrosis and non-union. This is why proximal fractures are managed and followed more aggressively.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 55-year-old woman has a distal radius fracture on plain film with suspected joint involvement. What is the main reason to obtain a CT before operative fixation?
options: To measure bone mineral density for osteoporosis
To exclude an associated soft-tissue abscess
To characterise intra-articular step, comminution and fragment position in 3D
To reduce the patient's radiation exposure compared with X-ray
To assess distal neurovascular flow directly
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: To characterise intra-articular step, comminution and fragment position in 3D
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: CT defines the degree of intra-articular extension, articular step, comminution and the position of fragments with multiplanar and 3D reconstruction, which plain films underestimate. This information guides the fixation strategy. CT does not measure bone density, does not lower radiation dose, and is not the tool for assessing vascular flow (that is clinical examination/Doppler/angiography).

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 24-year-old motorcyclist sustains a high-energy proximal tibial fracture. Six hours later he has severe pain in the calf that is worse on passive dorsiflexion of the toes, and the anterior compartment is tense. Distal pulses are palpable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent CT of the tibia to characterise the fracture
Elevate the limb and reassess in 4 hours
Apply a below-knee backslab and repeat plain films
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment indicate acute compartment syndrome, a limb-threatening emergency treated by urgent fasciotomy. Palpable pulses do not exclude it — pulselessness is a late sign, so waiting or imaging first is inappropriate.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 38-year-old man falls from a ladder and lands on his heels. Plain films show bilateral calcaneal fractures with flattening of Böhler's angle. Which additional injury must be specifically excluded?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: Axial-load calcaneal fractures from a fall from height are commonly bilateral and associated with thoracolumbar spinal fractures. The spine should be imaged in any such patient.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 45-year-old woman has an intra-articular distal tibial fracture from an axial load in a road traffic collision. Plain films suggest comminution of the plafond but the articular surface is hard to assess. What is the main role of CT in her management?
options: To confirm the diagnosis of fracture that the plain film missed
To exclude deep vein thrombosis in the injured limb
To quantify articular comminution, depression and fragment position for surgical planning
To assess ligamentous injury of the ankle
To measure limb-length discrepancy before mobilisation
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: To quantify articular comminution, depression and fragment position for surgical planning
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: This is a pilon (distal tibial plafond) fracture. CT characterises the intra-articular comminution, degree of depression and fragment position in 3D, which plain films underestimate, to plan internal fixation. It is not primarily for diagnosis, DVT, ligaments or limb length.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 27-year-old motorcyclist arrives after a high-speed collision. He is tachycardic (HR 128) and hypotensive (BP 82/50) with an obviously unstable pelvis on gentle springing. What is the most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Transfer immediately to CT for a pelvic angiogram to localise bleeding
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters and activate the major haemorrhage protocol
Insert a urethral catheter to monitor urine output
Take the patient directly to theatre for open reduction and internal fixation
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters and activate the major haemorrhage protocol
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: A haemodynamically unstable patient with an unstable pelvic ring fracture needs immediate haemorrhage control and resuscitation, NOT a trip to CT. A binder placed correctly over the greater trochanters reduces pelvic volume and tamponades bleeding; major haemorrhage protocol supports resuscitation before definitive embolisation/surgery. Catheterisation is contraindicated until urethral injury is excluded, and an unstable patient should not be delayed for CT.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: CT of the pelvis in a trauma patient shows widening of the pubic symphysis and disruption of the right sacroiliac joint. Which Young-Burgess pattern does this represent?
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: Symphyseal diastasis plus SI joint disruption is the hallmark of an anteroposterior compression (APC) or "open-book" injury, where AP force springs the ring open. This increases pelvic volume and carries a high risk of major haemorrhage. Lateral compression causes horizontal rami fractures with sacral impaction, and vertical shear displaces a hemipelvis vertically.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 40-year-old man with a pelvic fracture has blood at the urethral meatus and a high-riding prostate on examination. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Insert a urethral catheter to decompress the bladder
Arrange a retrograde urethrogram before any catheterisation
Insert a suprapubic catheter immediately without imaging
Perform a CT cystogram to exclude bladder rupture first
Reassure and observe, as these signs are non-specific
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: Arrange a retrograde urethrogram before any catheterisation
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: Blood at the meatus and a high-riding prostate indicate a probable urethral injury. Blind urethral catheterisation risks converting a partial tear into a complete disruption and is contraindicated until injury is excluded. A retrograde urethrogram is the appropriate investigation to define the urethra before deciding on catheter route.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) presents with a sudden, severely painful, pale, cold left leg. There are no palpable pulses below the femoral, and he now reports numbness and cannot wiggle his toes. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Arrange outpatient duplex ultrasound and start a statin
Commence supervised exercise therapy and clopidogrel
Give IV heparin and make an urgent vascular referral for revascularisation
Prescribe analgesia and review in the morning
Measure ABPI and arrange elective CT angiography in 2 weeks
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: Give IV heparin and make an urgent vascular referral for revascularisation
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: This is acute limb ischaemia (embolic, likely AF-related) with paraesthesia and paralysis indicating a threatened limb. It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate IV heparin and urgent vascular referral for embolectomy/thrombolysis — irreversible damage occurs after ~6 hours. Any delay (options A, D, E) or exercise therapy (B) risks limb loss.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 65-year-old diabetic man has calf pain on walking and a non-healing foot ulcer. His ABPI is measured at 1.3. Which statement best explains this result?
options: An ABPI of 1.3 excludes peripheral arterial disease
The ABPI is falsely elevated due to calcified, incompressible vessels
The ABPI confirms severe venous insufficiency
The reading indicates normal, healthy arterial flow requiring no imaging
The ABPI should prompt reassurance and discharge
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: The ABPI is falsely elevated due to calcified, incompressible vessels
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: In diabetes, medial arterial calcification makes vessels incompressible, producing a falsely high ABPI (>1.3). Given his claudication and non-healing ulcer, significant PAD/critical ischaemia is likely and must not be excluded on the basis of the raised ABPI — a toe-brachial index or CT run-off imaging is needed.

investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.question: A 68-year-old smoker with intermittent claudication undergoes CT peripheral angiography. It shows a single short 2 cm focal stenosis of the right superficial femoral artery with good distal run-off. What is the most appropriate role of this imaging finding in his management?
options: It confirms acute limb ischaemia requiring emergency embolectomy
It localises a focal lesion suitable for endovascular angioplasty/stenting
It rules out any need for antiplatelet or statin therapy
It indicates the leg has irreversible ischaemia
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.answer: It localises a focal lesion suitable for endovascular angioplasty/stenting
investigations__CT__MSK / Limbs.explanation: CT run-off maps the level and morphology of disease to plan revascularisation. A short focal stenosis with good distal run-off is well suited to endovascular angioplasty/stenting, whereas long occlusions or multilevel disease favour bypass. Best medical therapy (antiplatelet, statin, smoking cessation, supervised exercise) continues regardless, so option D is wrong; the picture is chronic, not acute or irreversible.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A 24-year-old is brought in after a high-speed RTC. On arrival he is tachycardic at 130 and hypotensive at 78/50 mmHg; a FAST scan shows free fluid in the abdomen and he remains hypotensive despite two units of blood. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Transfer to CT for an immediate whole-body pan-scan
Insert a chest drain and reassess
Obtain a supine chest and pelvic radiograph then repeat FAST
Arrange an MRI of the abdomen and pelvis
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: This is a persistent non-responder to resuscitation with a positive FAST indicating intra-abdominal haemorrhage. A haemodynamically unstable patient must not be delayed for CT — the scanner is a dangerous place for an exsanguinating patient. He needs immediate definitive haemorrhage control in theatre. CT (option A) is only appropriate once stable enough to tolerate it.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: Which component of a standard trauma pan-scan is correctly performed WITHOUT intravenous contrast?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: The head (and cervical spine) is imaged without contrast: acute intracranial blood is hyperdense on non-contrast CT, and adding contrast would obscure haemorrhage and is unnecessary for detecting brain or bony injury. Chest, abdomen and pelvis are all contrast-enhanced to demonstrate vascular injury, organ perfusion and active extravasation.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A stable polytrauma patient's arterial-phase abdominal CT shows a splenic laceration with a focal rounded area of high-density contrast identical to the aorta, with surrounding free fluid. What does this finding most likely represent and imply?
options: Normal splenic vasculature; no action needed
Active contrast extravasation, indicating ongoing bleeding requiring embolisation or surgery
A splenic cyst that can be managed conservatively
Beam-hardening artefact that should be ignored
Delayed-phase washout consistent with a benign lesion
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: Active contrast extravasation, indicating ongoing bleeding requiring embolisation or surgery
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: A focus of contrast matching the arterial blood pool (a 'blush') within an injured organ represents active extravasation of contrast from a bleeding vessel. It signifies ongoing haemorrhage and upgrades management from conservative observation towards angioembolisation or operative intervention, even if the patient is currently stable.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A 68-year-old with newly diagnosed colorectal cancer has a staging CT chest, abdomen and pelvis. Which intravenous contrast phase is standard for this examination and why?
options: Arterial phase (~25 s), to detect hypervascular liver lesions
Portal-venous phase (~60–70 s), for maximal liver parenchymal enhancement so hypodense metastases stand out
Delayed phase (~10 min), to assess urinary excretion
Dual-energy without any contrast, to characterise renal stones
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: Portal-venous phase (~60–70 s), for maximal liver parenchymal enhancement so hypodense metastases stand out
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: The portal-venous phase maximises normal liver enhancement, making hypovascular metastases conspicuous as relatively dark lesions, and also opacifies bowel wall, spleen and nodes. Arterial phase is added only for hypervascular tumours (HCC, neuroendocrine, renal), not as the default staging phase.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A staging CT for lung cancer incidentally shows a large anterior mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava with prominent chest-wall collateral veins, and the patient reports facial swelling. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: File as a routine incidental finding and await the MDT in two weeks
Recognise malignant SVC obstruction and escalate urgently for prompt oncological management
Arrange a repeat CT in three months for interval assessment
Reassure the patient as collateral veins indicate stable chronic disease
Ignore, as SVC findings do not affect staging
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: Recognise malignant SVC obstruction and escalate urgently for prompt oncological management
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: Mediastinal mass compressing the SVC with venous collaterals and facial swelling indicates malignant SVC obstruction — a time-critical complication that must be communicated and acted on urgently (steroids, oncology/radiotherapy or stenting), not deferred to routine staging pathways.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: During follow-up of a metastatic cancer on chemotherapy, the oncologist wants to quantify treatment response on serial CT scans. Which principle underlies the RECIST approach?
options: Whole-body tumour volume is segmented automatically on every scan
A limited number of target lesions are measured by longest diameter and compared over time
Only the metabolic SUV on PET is used to define response
Any new symptom automatically defines progression regardless of imaging
Response is judged solely by change in tumour density in Hounsfield units
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: A limited number of target lesions are measured by longest diameter and compared over time
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: RECIST standardises response assessment by selecting a small number of measurable target lesions, recording the longest diameter of each at baseline, and remeasuring on follow-up; the summed change classifies complete/partial response, stable disease or progression. It is anatomical/size-based, not primarily metabolic.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A 68-year-old man has an FDG-avid mediastinal lymph node on staging PET-CT for lung cancer. What is the most appropriate next step before this finding alters his management to palliative treatment?
options: Start palliative chemotherapy on the basis of the PET result
Obtain histological/cytological confirmation of the node (e.g. EBUS biopsy)
Give a therapeutic dose of radioiodine
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: Obtain histological/cytological confirmation of the node (e.g. EBUS biopsy)
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: FDG avidity is non-specific — inflammation, infection and granulomatous disease cause false positives. A positive PET finding that would upstage a patient and deny potentially curative treatment should be confirmed histologically before it changes management.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: Which physiological site of FDG uptake most limits assessment of intracranial metastases?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: The brain is an obligate glucose consumer and shows intense physiological FDG uptake, giving high background activity that can obscure cerebral metastases — dedicated MRI is preferred for brain assessment.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A patient's tumour is known to be strongly FDG-avid, but the scan is falsely negative. Which factor is the most likely reversible cause?
options: The patient was hyperglycaemic at the time of injection
The patient rested in a warm room
The tumour was 4 cm in size
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: The patient was hyperglycaemic at the time of injection
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: Elevated blood glucose competes with FDG for cellular uptake and lowers tumour avidity, causing false negatives. Controlling blood glucose and fasting before the scan is standard preparation.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: Which of the following is a recognised NON-oncological indication for FDG PET-CT?
options: Assessing large-vessel vasculitis or pyrexia of unknown origin
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: Assessing large-vessel vasculitis or pyrexia of unknown origin
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: FDG marks metabolically active inflammation, so PET-CT can map large-vessel vasculitis (e.g. GCA/Takayasu) and help localise the source in PUO. It is not used for fractures, osteoarthritis, appendicitis or general cancer screening.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: Immediately after an FDG PET-CT, what safety advice is most appropriate for the patient?
options: Avoid close, prolonged contact with pregnant women and young infants for the rest of the day
Remain in strict isolation for one week
Stop all regular medications for 48 hours
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.answer: Avoid close, prolonged contact with pregnant women and young infants for the rest of the day
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: The patient is transiently radioactive from the injected positron emitter, so brief avoidance of close contact with pregnant women and infants (and good hydration to clear tracer) is advised. Week-long isolation is unnecessary for 18F-FDG given its short half-life.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A 68-year-old man is due to have a CT-guided core biopsy of a peripheral lung nodule. Which single investigation is most important to perform immediately after the procedure before he is discharged?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: Pneumothorax is the most common significant complication of CT-guided lung biopsy and may develop or enlarge after the procedure. An erect chest X-ray (typically about an hour later) is performed to exclude a pneumothorax before discharge; a symptomatic or large one may need a chest drain.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A patient is listed for CT-guided liver biopsy of a suspicious lesion. Which pre-procedure finding should most prompt you to postpone the biopsy until corrected?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: Coagulation status must be checked and corrected before percutaneous biopsy. An INR of 2.6 markedly increases bleeding risk from a vascular organ like the liver; the procedure should be deferred until clotting is corrected and anticoagulants withheld. The other findings do not contraindicate the biopsy.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: A haematologist requests tissue from an enlarged retroperitoneal node to diagnose and subtype a suspected lymphoma. Which sampling method is most appropriate?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: Lymphoma classification requires assessment of tissue architecture and immunohistochemistry, so a core-needle biopsy (or excisional biopsy) is needed. FNA yields cells for cytology only and is usually insufficient to subtype lymphoma.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: Thirty minutes after a CT-guided lung biopsy a patient becomes acutely breathless with pleuritic chest pain and oxygen saturations of 88%. What is the most likely complication?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: Acute breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia soon after lung biopsy strongly suggest a pneumothorax, the commonest significant complication. Assess with examination and chest X-ray; a large or symptomatic pneumothorax may require a chest drain.

investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.question: Which of the following is a recognised but rare complication specifically related to the needle track in percutaneous biopsy?
investigations__CT__Whole Body / Special.explanation: Malignant cells can rarely be deposited along the needle track during biopsy, causing tumour seeding. It is uncommon but should be mentioned during consent. Contrast nephropathy and contrast anaphylaxis relate to contrast use, not the biopsy track itself.
